# 3. Sphere vs Surface Sphere

This one is very relevant to what we're doing.

Godot defines them as:

**Sphere**

> particles are emitted **inside the sphere volume**.

**Surface Sphere**

> particles are emitted **on the surface of the sphere**. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_cpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

In 2D, that essentially means:

### Sphere

```text

    ● ● ● ● ●
   ● ● ● ● ● ●
    ● ● ● ● ●
      ● ● ●
```

Particles can spawn anywhere inside the circular area.

### Surface Sphere

```text
       ● ● ●
     ●       ●
    ●         ●
     ●       ●
       ● ● ●
```

Particles spawn around the circumference.

### What the turbulence settings actually do

Think of turbulence as an invisible, moving **force field** that the particles fly through. It doesn't directly create more particles or make them larger; it changes their trajectories.

| Setting | What it actually does | Increasing it gives us |
|---|---|---|
| **Noise Strength** | How strong the noise field's directional forces are | More pronounced wandering/deflection |
| **Noise Scale** | Size/frequency of the noise pattern | Smaller, more rapidly changing movement |
| **Noise Speed X** | How quickly the noise field moves horizontally | More dynamic horizontal variation |
| **Noise Speed Y** | How quickly the noise field moves vertically | More dynamic vertical variation |
| **Influence Min/Max** | How strongly individual particles are affected | More/less particle deviation |
| **Influence over Life** | Changes that influence during the particle's lifetime | Lets us control *when* turbulence matters |

Godot's `Noise Strength` and `Noise Scale` control the turbulence field itself, while the influence determines how strongly particles respond to it.  

---

## Why huge values may have looked surprisingly similar

This is actually important.

You can increase:

```text
Noise Strength: 1 → 10
```

and expect:

> "HOLY SHIT, everything should fly everywhere."

But our particles are simultaneously affected by:

- their initial velocity
- damping
- tangential acceleration
- their relatively short lifetime
- the ribbon/ball constantly moving
- our Influence being only `0.08-0.18`

So **Influence is the big gatekeeper**.

If Influence stays low, increasing Noise Strength doesn't necessarily produce a dramatic visual difference.

Think of it like:

> Noise Strength = how strong the wind is  
> Influence = how much the particle actually feels the wind

A hurricane doesn't matter much if your particle only responds to 10% of it. 😄

---

# Our current turbulence values

I'd actually return to our original controlled values rather than chasing huge numbers:

0.15

Influence
Min: 0.08
Max: 0.18

Initial Displacement
0.0

Influence over Life
our existing curve
```

I like this because turbulence is **not supposed to be the main movement system**.

Our Tangential Accel is now providing some of the more noticeable lateral movement, while turbulence provides the subtle irregularity that prevents every particle trajectory from looking mathematically predictable.

And since you discovered that **±10 Tangential Accel creates a nice fuller effect**, I wouldn't make turbulence fight against it.

This is the tradeoff we just discovered.

Increasing acceleration:

> spreads particles → makes the trail fuller → looks more dynamic

but also:

That's why I agree with your instinct to keep **±10 rather than pushing it much higher**.

**"a cloud of 100 little balls."**

We want:

The distinction is subtle but really important for the identity of the effect.

And now that Hue Variation becomes more apparent when the particles separate more, I'd definitely keep it. It's doing exactly what it should: **subtle variation that becomes noticeable when you actually look at the particle field.**

mostly tiny fading remnants + occasional larger survivor

That last part is exactly where your `Lifetime Randomness = 0.15` helps us.

extends CharacterBody2D
## Ball-Movement-Prototyp für TowerJump.
## - Fällt durch Gravitation
## - Springt automatisch beim Aufkommen auf einer Plattform (kein Jump-Button)
## - Horizontale Steuerung über Touch-Zonen (linke/rechte Bildschirmhälfte)
## - Screen-Wrap an den seitlichen Bildschirmrändern

@export var radius: float = 30.0            ## Radius für Kreis-Placeholder UND Kollisionsform (einzige Quelle)
@export var gravity: float = 1800.0         ## Fallbeschleunigung (px/s^2)
@export var jump_velocity: float = -1200.0  ## Vertikale Sprunggeschwindigkeit (negativ = nach oben)
@export_category("Horizontal Movement")
@export var max_horizontal_speed: float = 600.0
@export var horizontal_acceleration: float = 2200.0
@export var horizontal_deceleration: float = 1700.0

## Aktuelle Steuerrichtung, binär: -1 = voll links, 0 = keine, 1 = voll rechts
var input_direction: float = 0.0

## Aktive Touches während des Haltens: Touch-Index -> Seite (-1 links, 1 rechts).
## Wird in _input() über ScreenTouch/ScreenDrag gepflegt, damit Mehrfach-Touch
## (z.B. beide Bildschirmhälften gleichzeitig) korrekt erkannt wird.
var _touch_sides: Dictionary = {}

@onready var _collision_shape: CollisionShape2D = $CollisionShape2D

## Pflegt _touch_sides anhand von Touch-Press/-Release und -Drag-Events, damit
## auch ein über die Bildschirmmitte gezogener Finger die Seite aktualisiert.
func _input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event is InputEventScreenTouch:
		if event.pressed:
			_touch_sides[event.index] = _touch_side(event.position.x)
		else:
			_touch_sides.erase(event.index)
	elif event is InputEventScreenDrag:
		if _touch_sides.has(event.index):
			_touch_sides[event.index] = _touch_side(event.position.x)

## Ordnet eine x-Koordinate der linken (-1) oder rechten (1) Bildschirmhälfte zu.
func _touch_side(x: float) -> int:
	return -1 if x < get_viewport_rect().size.x * 0.5 else 1

func _ready() -> void:
	# Kollisionsform zur Laufzeit aus `radius` generieren, damit es nur eine
	# Quelle für den Ball-Radius gibt (statt zusätzlich in der .tscn zu duplizieren).
	var shape := CircleShape2D.new()
	shape.radius = radius
	_collision_shape.shape = shape
	add_to_group("player_ball") # Ermöglicht Coin.gd die Erkennung des Balls per Duck-Typing-Gruppe


func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	input_direction = _read_input_direction()

	# --- Gravitation ---
	velocity.y += gravity * delta

	# --- Horizontal movement with momentum ---
	var input_direction := Input.get_axis("ui_left", "ui_right")

	if abs(input_direction) > 0.01:
		var target_speed := input_direction * max_horizontal_speed

		# Accelerate toward the desired direction.
		velocity.x = move_toward(
			velocity.x,
			target_speed,
			horizontal_acceleration * delta
		)
	else:
		# No input: gradually lose horizontal momentum.
		velocity.x = move_toward(
			velocity.x,
			0.0,
			horizontal_deceleration * delta
		)

	move_and_slide()

	# --- Auto-Bounce: beim Aufkommen automatisch abspringen ---
	if is_on_floor():
		velocity.y = jump_velocity * _landed_jump_multiplier()

	_screen_wrap()

## Ermittelt beim Aufkommen die Plattform unter dem Ball und liefert deren
## Sprunggeschwindigkeits-Multiplikator (>1 nur bei Spring-Plattformen, siehe
## platform.gd). Duck-Typing über has_method(), damit ball.gd nichts über
## Plattform-Varianten wissen muss - Seiteneffekte wie das Wegbrechen einer
## brüchigen Plattform passieren dabei innerhalb von Platform.on_ball_landed().
func _landed_jump_multiplier() -> float:
	for i in get_slide_collision_count():
		var collider: Object = get_slide_collision(i).get_collider()
		if collider is Node and collider.has_method("on_ball_landed"):
			return collider.on_ball_landed()
	return 1.0

## Lässt den Ball auf der Gegenseite wieder auftauchen, wenn er den Bildschirm seitlich verlässt.
func _screen_wrap() -> void:
	var screen_width: float = get_viewport_rect().size.x
	if global_position.x < -radius:
		global_position.x = screen_width + radius
	elif global_position.x > screen_width + radius:
		global_position.x = -radius

## Liefert die Steuerrichtung (-1, 0 oder 1). Am PC gibt es keinen Touchscreen,
## daher wird dort ersatzweise über die Pfeiltasten (ui_left/ui_right) gesteuert.
func _read_input_direction() -> float:
	if should_use_touch_controls():
		return _read_touch_direction()
	return _read_keyboard_direction()

## Wertet _touch_sides aus: Touches auf nur einer Seite ergeben volle Auslenkung
## dorthin. Sind beide Seiten gleichzeitig berührt, heben sie sich zu 0 auf -
## dieselbe Kollisionsregel wie bei gleichzeitig gedrückten Pfeiltasten unten.
func _read_touch_direction() -> float:
	var has_left := false
	var has_right := false
	for side in _touch_sides.values():
		if side < 0:
			has_left = true
		else:
			has_right = true
	if has_left == has_right:
		return 0.0
	return -1.0 if has_left else 1.0

## Liefert bei gedrückter Pfeiltaste sofort volle Auslenkung. Bei gleichzeitig
## gedrückten ui_left/ui_right heben sich beide Richtungen zu 0 auf.
func _read_keyboard_direction() -> float:
	var dir: float = 0.0
	if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_left"):
		dir -= 1.0
	if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_right"):
		dir += 1.0
	return dir

## Entscheidet, ob die Touch-Zonen genutzt werden sollen (echtes mobiles Gerät)
## oder die Tastatur-Ersatzsteuerung (Editor/Desktop).
## OS.has_feature("editor") ist bei einem per F5 aus dem Editor gestarteten
## Spiel ebenfalls wahr, daher zusätzlich über OS.has_feature("mobile")
## gegenprüfen, damit ein Export mit fälschlich aktivem "editor"-Feature
## trotzdem korrekt die Touch-Steuerung nutzt.
static func should_use_touch_controls() -> bool:
	if OS.has_feature("editor"):
		return false
	return OS.has_feature("mobile")

Yes. **One final experiment - and this time we're going in a genuinely different direction.**

We're going to leave the particle physics **100% untouched** and use a **CanvasItem shader purely to change the visual intensity of the existing particles based on the ball's actual speed**.

Godot's particle rendering passes the particle `COLOR` into the CanvasItem shader, and particle instances also expose lifetime phase through `INSTANCE_CUSTOM.y`. We can therefore modify the appearance without modifying the particle motion. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?highlight=MODULATE&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

## The idea

```text
Ball velocity
      ↓
ball_trail.gd
      ↓
shader uniform: energy
      ↓
existing particles
      ↓
same sparks / same movement
but stronger visual energy
```

No:

- `amount_ratio`
- `Inherit Velocity Ratio`
- extra particle spawning
- velocity changes
- Process Material changes

---

# 1. Add a shader to `TrailParticles`

Select:

```text
TrailVisual
└── TrailParticles
```

On **TrailParticles → Material**, create:

**New ShaderMaterial**

Then inside the ShaderMaterial create a:

**New Shader**

Open it and replace everything with:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;
render_mode unshaded;

uniform float energy_strength = 1.0;

void fragment() {
	vec4 tex_color = texture(TEXTURE, UV);

	float lifetime_phase = INSTANCE_CUSTOM.y;

	// Subtle individual spark variation.
	float spark = 0.88 + 0.12 * sin(lifetime_phase * 18.0 + INSTANCE_CUSTOM.x * 3.0);

	float intensity = mix(1.0, energy_strength, spark);

	COLOR = tex_color * COLOR;
	COLOR.rgb *= intensity;
}
```

### Why this should behave differently

The important line is:

```glsl
COLOR = tex_color * COLOR;
```

We're preserving the particle texture **and** the color coming from your existing particle system.

Then:

```glsl
COLOR.rgb *= intensity;
```

only changes its visual brightness.

So your:

- scale
- scale curve
- alpha curve
- turbulence
- tangential acceleration
- spread
- lifetime
- randomness
- particle positions

remain untouched.

The shader is only changing what those existing particles **look like** when rendered. CanvasItem shaders are specifically used for rendering 2D elements, and shader parameters can be updated from GDScript. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# 2. Now the important part: feed it the ball speed

In your `ball_trail.gd`, add this underneath your existing variables:

```gdscript
@export_category("Particle Energy")
@export var energy_speed_start: float = 300.0
@export var energy_speed_full: float = 900.0
@export var energy_max_strength: float = 1.8
@export var energy_response_speed: float = 8.0

var _particle_energy: float = 1.0

@onready var _trail_particles: GPUParticles2D = $TrailParticles
```

You already have:

```gdscript
@onready var _energy_line: Line2D = $EnergyLine
```

so simply put the new `@onready` underneath it.

---

# 3. Add this to `_process()`

You currently have:

```gdscript
func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var ball := get_parent()

	if ball == null:
		return

	var current_world_position: Vector2 = ball.global_position
```

Immediately after `current_world_position`, add:

```gdscript
	var ball_speed: float = ball.velocity.length()

	var energy_t: float = inverse_lerp(
		energy_speed_start,
		energy_speed_full,
		ball_speed
	)

	energy_t = clamp(energy_t, 0.0, 1.0)

	# Smooth response instead of an abrupt brightness jump.
	energy_t = energy_t * energy_t * (3.0 - 2.0 * energy_t)

	var target_energy: float = lerp(
		1.0,
		energy_max_strength,
		energy_t
	)

	_particle_energy = lerp(
		_particle_energy,
		target_energy,
		1.0 - exp(-energy_response_speed * delta)
	)

	var particle_material := _trail_particles.material as ShaderMaterial

	if particle_material != null:
		particle_material.set_shader_parameter(
			"energy_strength",
			_particle_energy
		)
```

Godot supports changing a shader uniform through `ShaderMaterial.set_shader_parameter()`. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_shadermaterial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# 4. What we're starting with

Leave these values exactly as:

```text
Energy Speed Start:       300
Energy Speed Full:        900
Energy Max Strength:      1.8
Energy Response Speed:    8
```

So conceptually:

```text
Ball speed        Particle brightness

0-300             1.0×
600               ~1.2×
900+              1.8×
```

But because of the smoothstep response, it won't feel like a mechanical brightness slider.

We're **not trying to make the entire particle cloud brighter**.

The shader deliberately has:

```

so individual particles have slightly different intensity.

Then the ball speed controls how much that existing variation is amplified.

That should hopefully give us something more like:

### Fast

without turning everything into:

which is exactly the problem we had with velocity-based approaches.

If the shader approach works, you should notice the sparks becoming **more luminous and energetic**, while their shapes and trajectories remain the same.

### 1. We should artificially vary the ball speed again

If the ball normally sits around ~600 px/s, then our shader response won't have much range to react to. We *can* test it at the normal speed, but that only tells us what happens around that one point.

For this final experiment, I'd temporarily use the same speed test as before:

- **1200** = fast

So yes: temporarily make the ball faster again. If 1200 is annoying to control, that's fine - we're only using it as a visual test.

---

### 2. The shader error is my mistake

You're absolutely right.

`INSTANCE_CUSTOM` **is available in the CanvasItem shader's vertex stage**, but I incorrectly tried to access it directly inside `fragment()`. Godot's shader documentation specifically notes that built-ins like `INSTANCE_CUSTOM` need to be passed from `vertex()` to `fragment()` with a `varying` when needed there. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

So let's fix that rather than adding unnecessary complexity.

Replace the shader I gave you with this:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;
render_mode unshaded;

uniform float energy_strength = 1.0;

varying float particle_phase;

void vertex() {
	particle_phase = INSTANCE_CUSTOM.y;
}

void fragment() {
	vec4 tex_color = texture(TEXTURE, UV);

	float spark = 0.88 + 0.12 * sin(
		particle_phase * 18.0
	);

	float intensity = mix(
		1.0,
		energy_strength,
		spark
	);

	COLOR = tex_color * COLOR;
	COLOR.rgb *= intensity;
}
```

The important change is:

```glsl
varying float particle_phase;

void vertex() {
	particle_phase = INSTANCE_CUSTOM.y;
}
```

and then the fragment shader uses:

```glsl
particle_phase
```

instead of trying to access `INSTANCE_CUSTOM` directly.

Godot documents `INSTANCE_CUSTOM.y` as the particle's lifetime phase (`0.0 → 1.0`) when used for particles, so this is exactly what we want for a little individual spark variation. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

---

Yes - and I think these are **two worthwhile final fixes**, especially the second one. The viewport stretching is clearly a bug, not an artistic feature.

## 1. The taper / closed end

I **wouldn't change the geometry just because `aura_alpha` went from the old value to `0.24`**.

Higher alpha can make the existing end *look* more connected, but it doesn't actually close the geometry. Your main ribbon already tapers to `end_width = 2`, and the aura is intentionally fading toward the end.

So I'd first try only a **small alpha increase**, something like:

```gdscript
@export var aura_alpha: float = 0.28
```

rather than jumping much higher.

If `0.28` makes the endpoint feel more like a closed tail without making the aura too dominant, **keep it**.

If it still visually looks open, I would **not keep increasing alpha**. At that point the proper fix is a tiny terminal cap/closure in the aura geometry rather than making the whole aura brighter.

So:

> **Try 0.28. If it doesn't solve it, leave 0.24 and we'll consider the taper visually good enough.**

---

# 2. The viewport stretching absolutely should be fixed

This one I definitely want to fix.

The reason is that your trail stores **world positions** in `_points`, then uses those positions to build the ribbon. Godot's `to_local()` converts those global positions into the TrailVisual's local space. That's normally exactly what we want. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_node2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

But if there is ever a **large discontinuity between two stored positions**, your custom polygon happily connects them with one enormous segment.

That's what you're seeing:

```text
normal:

●
 \
  \
   \____

bad:

●
 \
  \
   \___________________________________________
                                               \
                                                ●
```

The drawing system doesn't know that a giant connection is unintended; it simply draws the polygon between the two points. Custom drawing is cached from the points we provide until we redraw it. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/2d/custom_drawing_in_2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

### The clean fix

We should add a **maximum allowed distance between consecutive trail points**.

If the ball suddenly jumps/teleports a large distance - including leaving/re-entering the viewport or any future camera/wrap situation - we simply reset the trail instead of drawing a giant connection.

---

## Add this to your Trail settings

Under:

```gdscript
@export var min_distance: float = 3.0
```

add:

```gdscript
@export var max_segment_distance: float = 120.0
```

I'd start with **120 px**.

Your normal movement between frames should be nowhere near that, so this won't affect the regular trail.

---

## Then change this section

You currently have:

```gdscript
var last_world_position: Vector2 = _points[0]

if current_world_position.distance_to(last_world_position) >= min_distance:
	_points.push_front(current_world_position)

	while _points.size() > max_points:
		_points.pop_back()
```

Replace it with:

```gdscript
var last_world_position: Vector2 = _points[0]

var distance_from_trail: float = current_world_position.distance_to(
	last_world_position
)

# If the ball jumped an unusually large distance, do not connect
# the old trail to the new position.
if distance_from_trail > max_segment_distance:
	_points.clear()
	_points.append(current_world_position)
	_update_energy_line()
	queue_redraw()
	return

if distance_from_trail >= min_distance:
	_points.push_front(current_world_position)

	while _points.size() > max_points:
		_points.pop_back()
```

### What happens now

Normal movement:

```text
distance = 5 px
→ normal trail
```

Fast movement:

```text
distance = 20 px
→ normal trail
```

Unexpected jump:

```text
distance = 500 px
→ OLD TRAIL DELETED
→ new trail starts at ball
```

So instead of:

> **GIANT NEON LINE ACROSS THE ENTIRE SCREEN**

you get:

> **trail disappears for a moment and cleanly starts again at the ball.**

That's exactly what we want.

---

### One thing I would NOT do

I wouldn't simply clear the trail whenever the ball leaves the viewport.

That would tie the visual system to the viewport and could cause weird behavior later when we introduce the tower camera/scrolling.

The **distance safeguard is much more robust** because it solves the actual problem: an impossible jump between two trail samples.

---

## So my final values for this pass

**Main ribbon:**

```text
max_points: 18
min_distance: 3
max_segment_distance: 120
```

**Outer aura:**

```text
aura_alpha: 0.28
```

Test those two changes independently.

If `0.28` makes the taper nicer → keep it.

If it doesn't → **go back to 0.24**, because I don't want to sacrifice the beautiful subtle outer aura just to force the endpoint closed.

And the `max_segment_distance` fix I'd **definitely keep**. It doesn't change the normal appearance of the trail at all; it only prevents pathological geometry from being drawn.

extends StaticBody2D


enum PlatformType {
	NORMAL, 
	MOVING, 
	BREAKABLE,
	SPRING,
}

@export var width: float = 220.0
@export var height: float = 20.0


var width_scale: float = 1.0



@export_group("Beweglich")
@export var move_radius: float = 90.0
@export var move_speed: float = 1.6

@export_group("Brüchig")
@export var breakable_warning_duration: float = 0.3
@export var breakable_flicker_color: Color = Color(1.0, 0.35, 0.25, 1.0)
@export var breakable_wobble_amplitude: float = 5.0

@export_group("Spring")
@export var spring_multiplier: float = 1.75 

const NEON_COLOR := Color(0.0, 5.0, 7.0, 1.0)
const PLATFORM_BODY_COLOR := Color("#0B111B")

const BEVEL := 4.0
const EDGE_HEIGHT := 4.0
const EDGE_INSET := 1.0

var platform_type: PlatformType = PlatformType.NORMAL

var _base_position: Vector2 = Vector2.ZERO
var _move_phase: float = 0.0
var _is_breaking: bool = false
var _broken: bool = false

@onready var _collision_shape: CollisionShape2D = $CollisionShape2D
@onready var _visual: Polygon2D = $Visual

@onready var _neon_edge: Polygon2D = $NeonEdge

func _ready() -> void:
	_collision_shape.one_way_collision = true
	_apply_geometry()


func _apply_geometry() -> void:
	var shape := RectangleShape2D.new()
	shape.size = Vector2(width * width_scale, height)
	_collision_shape.shape = shape

	var hw: float = half_width()
	var hh: float = height * 0.5

	_visual.polygon = PackedVector2Array([
		Vector2(-hw + BEVEL, -hh),
		Vector2(hw - BEVEL, -hh),

		Vector2(hw, -hh + BEVEL),
		Vector2(hw, hh - BEVEL),

		Vector2(hw - BEVEL, hh),
		Vector2(-hw + BEVEL, hh),

		Vector2(-hw, hh - BEVEL),
		Vector2(-hw, -hh + BEVEL)
	])
	
	_visual.color = PLATFORM_BODY_COLOR

	_neon_edge.polygon = PackedVector2Array([
		Vector2(-hw + BEVEL + EDGE_INSET, -hh),
		Vector2(hw - BEVEL - EDGE_INSET, -hh),

		Vector2(hw - EDGE_INSET, -hh + BEVEL),
		Vector2(hw - EDGE_INSET, -hh + EDGE_HEIGHT),

		Vector2(-hw + EDGE_INSET, -hh + EDGE_HEIGHT),
		Vector2(-hw + EDGE_INSET, -hh + BEVEL)
	])

	_neon_edge.color = NEON_COLOR

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	if platform_type == PlatformType.MOVING and not _is_breaking and not _broken:
		_move_phase += move_speed * delta
		position.x = _base_position.x + sin(_move_phase) * move_radius

func half_width() -> float:
	return width * width_scale * 0.5


func spawn_as(type: PlatformType, new_position: Vector2, new_width_scale: float = 1.0) -> void:
	platform_type = type
	width_scale = new_width_scale
	global_position = new_position
	_base_position = new_position
	_move_phase = randf_range(0.0, TAU)
	_is_breaking = false
	_broken = false
	modulate = Color.WHITE
	_collision_shape.disabled = false
	visible = true
	_apply_geometry()


func on_ball_landed() -> float:
	if platform_type == PlatformType.BREAKABLE:
		_start_breaking()
		return 1.0
	if platform_type == PlatformType.SPRING:
		return spring_multiplier
	return 1.0



func _start_breaking() -> void:
	if _is_breaking or _broken:
		return
	_is_breaking = true

	var tween := create_tween()
	tween.tween_property(self, "modulate", breakable_flicker_color, breakable_warning_duration)
	tween.parallel().tween_method(_apply_wobble, 0.0, 1.0, breakable_warning_duration)
	tween.tween_callback(_break)

func _apply_wobble(t: float) -> void:
	position.x = _base_position.x + sin(t * TAU * 6.0) * breakable_wobble_amplitude * (1.0 - t)

func _break() -> void:
	_is_breaking = false
	_broken = true
	position.x = _base_position.x
	_collision_shape.disabled = true
	visible = false

A uniform controlled by `Platform.gd`:

Platform Body Shader:

shader_type canvas_item;

uniform float platform_height = 20.0;
uniform float reflection_height = 2.0;

void fragment() {
    vec2 uv = UV;

    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 1. PIXEL POSITION
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float pixel_y = uv.y * platform_height;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 2. VERY DARK BASE MATERIAL
    // --------------------------------------------------

    vec3 upper_body = vec3(0.012, 0.028, 0.045);
    vec3 lower_body = vec3(0.003, 0.006, 0.010);

    float body_gradient = smoothstep(
        2.0,
        platform_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    vec3 body = mix(
        upper_body,
        lower_body,
        body_gradient
    );


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 3. SOFT CYAN LIGHT RECEIVED FROM NEON
    // --------------------------------------------------

    vec3 cyan = vec3(0.0, 0.28, 0.40);

    float reflection = 1.0 - smoothstep(
        0.0,
        reflection_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    reflection *= 0.16;

    body += cyan * reflection;


	// --------------------------------------------------
	// 4. SUBTLE UPPER MATERIAL HIGHLIGHT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float upper_highlight = 1.0 - smoothstep(
	    0.0,
	    1.5,
	    pixel_y
	);

	upper_highlight *= 0.10;

	body += vec3(0.10, 0.14, 0.16) * upper_highlight;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 5. LOWER EDGE DARKENING
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float lower_edge = smoothstep(
        platform_height - 2.0,
        platform_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    body *= 1.0 - lower_edge * 0.45;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 6. SUBTLE SIDE EDGE SHADING
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float side_edge = min(uv.x, 1.0 - uv.x);

shader_type canvas_item;

uniform float platform_height = 20.0;
uniform float reflection_height = 2.0;
instance uniform float landing_pulse: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
instance uniform float landing_energy: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;

void fragment() {
    vec2 uv = UV;

    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 1. PIXEL POSITION
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float pixel_y = uv.y * platform_height;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 2. VERY DARK BASE MATERIAL
    // --------------------------------------------------

    vec3 upper_body = vec3(0.012, 0.028, 0.045);
    vec3 lower_body = vec3(0.003, 0.006, 0.010);

    float body_gradient = smoothstep(
        2.0,
        platform_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    vec3 body = mix(
        upper_body,
        lower_body,
        body_gradient
    );


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 3. SOFT CYAN LIGHT RECEIVED FROM NEON
    // --------------------------------------------------

    vec3 cyan = vec3(0.0, 0.28, 0.40);

    float reflection = 1.0 - smoothstep(
        0.0,
        reflection_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    reflection *= 0.16;

    body += cyan * reflection;


	// --------------------------------------------------
	// 4. SUBTLE UPPER MATERIAL HIGHLIGHT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float upper_highlight = 1.0 - smoothstep(
	    0.0,
	    1.5,
	    pixel_y
	);

	upper_highlight *= 0.10;

	body += vec3(0.10, 0.14, 0.16) * upper_highlight;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 5. LOWER EDGE DARKENING
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float lower_edge = smoothstep(
        platform_height - 2.0,
        platform_height,
        pixel_y
    );

    body *= 1.0 - lower_edge * 0.45;


    // --------------------------------------------------
    // 6. SUBTLE SIDE EDGE SHADING
    // --------------------------------------------------

    float side_edge = min(uv.x, 1.0 - uv.x);

    float edge_darkening = 1.0 - smoothstep(
        0.0,
        0.025,
        side_edge
    );

    body *= 1.0 - edge_darkening * 0.12;
	
	// --------------------------------------------------
	// 7. LANDING ENERGY WAVE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	vec3 landing_color = vec3(0.012, 0.065, 0.14);

	float wave_position = landing_pulse;

	// Soft outer energy field.
	float wave_outer = 1.0 - smoothstep(
	    0.04,
	    0.18,
	    abs(pixel_y / platform_height - wave_position)
	);

	// Narrow brighter center.
	float wave_core = 1.0 - smoothstep(
	    0.01,
	    0.055,
	    abs(pixel_y / platform_height - wave_position)
	);

	// Combine the soft field and bright core.
	float wave = wave_outer * 0.35 + wave_core * 0.65;

	// Fade the wave in at the top and completely out after the bottom.
	float wave_presence = smoothstep(
	    0.0,
	    0.08,
	    landing_pulse
	);

	wave *= wave_presence;

	body += landing_color * wave;
	
	// --------------------------------------------------
	// INTERNAL ENERGY DIAGNOSTIC
	// --------------------------------------------------

	body = vec3(UV.x, 0.0, 0.0);

    // --------------------------------------------------
    // OUTPUT
    // --------------------------------------------------

    COLOR = vec4(body, 1.0);
}

	float f1_y = 0.25;

	float f1 = 1.0 - smoothstep(

		0.045,

	);

	// --------------------------------------------------

	// --------------------------------------------------

	float f2_x = fract(
		energy_phase * 2.13 + 0.31
	) * 0.90 + 0.05;

	float f2_y = 0.68;

	float f2_distance = length(

		)
	);

	float f2 = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.012,
		0.040,

	);

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// FRAGMENT GROUP 3
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float f3_x = fract(
		energy_phase * 2.91 + 0.63
	) * 0.90 + 0.05;

	float f3_y = 0.48;

	float f3_distance = length(
		vec2(
			x - f3_x,
			y - f3_y
		)
	);

	float f3 = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.010,
		0.035,
		f3_distance
	);

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// SMALL STREAKS
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float streak1_center = fract(
		energy_phase * 1.73 + 0.17
	);

	float streak1_y = 0.38;

	float streak1_x_distance = abs(
		x - streak1_center
	);

	float streak1_y_distance = abs(
		y - streak1_y
	);

	float streak1 =
		(1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.035, streak1_y_distance)) *
		(1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.045, streak1_x_distance));

	// Break the streak so it isn't a continuous line.
	float streak1_break =
		sin(
			x * 95.0 +
			energy_phase * 18.0
		);

	streak1 *= smoothstep(
		-0.15,
		0.35,
		streak1_break
	);

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// COMBINE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float fragments =
		f1 * 1.0 +
		f2 * 0.75 +
		f3 * 0.55 +
		streak1 * 0.35;

	vec3 energy_color = vec3(
		0.0,
		0.75,
		1.0
	);

	body += energy_color * fragments * energy_active;

    // --------------------------------------------------
    // OUTPUT
    // --------------------------------------------------

    COLOR = vec4(body, 1.0);
}

# 3. Give `LandingEnergy` its shader

Create a new ShaderMaterial for `LandingEnergy` and use:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

render_mode unshaded, blend_add;

instance uniform float landing_energy: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
instance uniform float platform_width = 220.0;

varying float platform_x;
varying float platform_y;

void vertex() {
	platform_x = VERTEX.x;
	platform_y = VERTEX.y;
}

void fragment() {

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// PLATFORM COORDINATES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float half_width = platform_width * 0.5;

	float x = (platform_x + half_width) / platform_width;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// SURFACE HEIGHT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	// Platform top is around -10 for a 20px platform.
	// The LandingEnergy polygon sits above that.
	float surface_y = platform_y + 10.0;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// TRAVEL POSITION
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float travel_x = landing_energy;

	// Slight vertical wandering.
	float center_y =
		-3.0
		+ sin(landing_energy * TAU * 2.0) * 2.0;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// MAIN ENERGY SPARK
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float dx = x - travel_x;

	float dy =
		surface_y - center_y;

// Make the main spark irregular instead of perfectly straight.
	float wobble =
		sin(x * 35.0 + landing_energy * 18.0) * 2.0;

	dy += wobble;

float distance_to_spark = sqrt(
		dx * dx * 220.0 * 220.0 +
		dy * dy
	);

float spark = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		2.0,
		7.0,
		distance_to_spark
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// SOFT ENERGY AURA
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float aura = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		5.0,
		15.0,
		abs(dy)
	);

	aura *= 0.30;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// SHORT VERTICAL ELECTRICAL BRANCHES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float branch_pattern =
		sin(
			x * 48.0 +
			landing_energy * 25.0
		);

	float branch_mask = smoothstep(
		0.72,
		0.92,
		branch_pattern
	);

	float branch_distance =
		abs(dy + branch_pattern * 5.0);

	float branches = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.0,
		4.0,
		branch_distance
	);

	branches *= branch_mask;
	branches *= spark;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// FADE AFTER THE SPARK PASSES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float fade =
		1.0 - smoothstep(
			0.82,
			1.0,
			landing_energy
		);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// COLOR
	// --------------------------------------------------

	vec3 energy_color = vec3(
		0.0,
		0.85,
		1.0
	);

	float intensity =
		spark +
		aura +
		branches * 0.6;

	intensity *= fade;

COLOR = vec4(
		energy_color * intensity,
		intensity
	);
}
```

### One thing I intentionally did differently

We're **not trying to generate a realistic lightning simulation**.

We're creating a graphic game effect:

> **bright core + soft aura + irregular little branches**

That is much more likely to read as electricity at your game's scale.

And `blend_add` is appropriate here because the effect is meant to add luminous energy over the platform rather than replace its colors. Godot's CanvasItem shaders support additive blending directly. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/de/4.x/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

# 4. Connect it to your existing landing function

This is where the new effect actually becomes alive.

At the beginning of `_play_landing_pulse()` add:

```gdscript

		"landing_energy",
		0.0
	)
```

Then your tween structure becomes:

```gdscript
func _play_landing_pulse() -> void:
	_neon_edge.color = NEON_COLOR

	_visual.set_instance_shader_parameter(
		"landing_pulse",
		0.0
	)

	_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
		"landing_energy",
		0.0
	)

	var tween := create_tween()

	tween.set_parallel(true)

	# --------------------------------------------------
	# NEON EDGE
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_property(
		_neon_edge,
		"color",
		LANDING_EDGE_COLOR,
		0.08
	).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_EXPO).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

# --------------------------------------------------
	# BODY LANDING ILLUMINATION
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_method(
		func(value: float) -> void:
			_visual.set_instance_shader_parameter(
				"landing_pulse",
				value
			),
		0.0,
		1.0,
		1.15
	).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

# --------------------------------------------------
	# SURFACE ENERGY
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_method(
		func(value: float) -> void:
			_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
				"landing_energy",
				value
			),
		0.0,
		1.0,
		0.75
	).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_IN_OUT)

tween.set_parallel(false)

# --------------------------------------------------
	# NEON EDGE RECOVERY
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_property(
		_neon_edge,
		"color",
		NEON_COLOR,
		1.92
	).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

# --------------------------------------------------
	# BODY RECOVERY
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_method(
		func(value: float) -> void:
			_visual.set_instance_shader_parameter(
				"landing_pulse",
				value
			),
		1.0,
		0.0,
		1.90
	).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

# --------------------------------------------------
	# RESET SURFACE ENERGY
	# --------------------------------------------------

	tween.tween_callback(
		func() -> void:
			_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
				"landing_energy",
				0.0
			)
			_visual.set_instance_shader_parameter(
				"landing_pulse",
				0.0
			)
	)
```

**Then**

          ·    ·
```

**Then nothing.**

The body illumination and NeonEdge pulse continue doing their existing 2-second recovery while the flashy surface energy is much faster.

### The current effect has three problems

1. **It looks like an object floating above the platform.**  
   Because we're drawing a separate bright shape in a separate `Polygon2D`, it reads as *"something placed on top"* rather than energy being emitted by the platform.

2. **The reset is visible.**  
   Because `landing_energy` starts at `0` and the shader immediately evaluates that state, the effect exists before the animation reaches the landing point. On a wide platform, you can therefore see the "spark" sitting there waiting. That's especially bad.

3. **The motion isn't physically connected to the landing.**  
   We're effectively saying:
   > "Here is an energy object; move it from left to right."

   What we actually want is:
   > **"The landing generates energy at the contact point, and that energy propagates through the platform surface."**

That's an important distinction.

## So I would NOT polish the current effect

I wouldn't spend another 30 minutes tweaking the current wandering ball.

We should change the **animation model**, not the colors.

### Better architecture

The surface should be treated as an **energy propagation field**, not as a moving sprite/object.

Something conceptually like:

```text
LAND
              ↓
──────────────●──────────────
              │
          impact energy
              ↓
──────────────✦──────────────→
            ╱ │ ╲
           ╱  │  ╲
──────────╱───┼───╲──────────→
```

The important thing is that the effect's **origin is the actual landing point**.

Then:

```text
t = 0.00

────────────●────────────────
             ✦
```

↓

```text
t = 0.15

─────────────╲✦──────────────
               ╲
```

↓

```text
t = 0.35

──────────────────╲─✦───────
                    ╲╱
```

↓

```text
t = 0.55

──────────────────────────✦─
```

↓

```text
t = 0.70

────────────────────────────
```

No object exists before the landing.

No "ball" is waiting at the beginning.

No hard reset is visible.

# And there's another important change I'd make

**Don't force it to travel left → right globally.**

The landing point should determine the origin.

If the ball lands here:

```text
──────────────────●────────────
```

energy could travel:

```text
──────────────────✦───→───────
```

If it lands here:

```text
──────●────────────────────────
```

then:

```text
──────✦──────→─────────────────
```

And potentially we can have a **tiny amount of energy scatter backwards**, so it feels like the impact actually happened:

```text
────────╲─●─╱──────────────────
         ╲│╱
          ✦──────→
```

That would make the effect feel much more connected to the ball.

## Can a shader actually do this convincingly?

**Yes.**

And this is where our previous shader experiments actually taught us something useful.

The shader doesn't need to simulate complicated electricity.

We already know our platform shader can successfully render:

- horizontal positions
- vertical gradients
- animated values
- thin streaks
- localized energy

And Godot's CanvasItem shader gives us local-space `VERTEX` coordinates, so we can build the field directly around a controlled origin rather than trying to make a fake particle-like object. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The trick is to give the effect **three components**:

### A. Impact flash

Very short:

```text
        ╱│╲
─────────✦─────────
        ╲│╱
```

### B. Propagation core

A bright irregular front:

```text
──────────────────╲✦╱────────
```

### C. Residual energy

A very brief fading trace behind it:

```text
──────────────···╲✦──────────
```

That third part is what makes it feel like **energy traveled through the surface**, rather than a glowing dot simply moving across it.

---

# And we can eliminate the reset problem completely

This is the most important part.

Instead of the shader drawing something meaningful at:

```gdscript
landing_energy = 0.0
```

we make the effect **completely invisible at 0**.

Something like:

```text
energy = 0.00 → invisible
energy = 0.01 → tiny impact
energy = 0.10 → impact expands
energy = 0.30 → propagation
energy = 0.70 → propagation
energy = 0.95 → fading
energy = 1.00 → invisible
```

So the animation itself becomes:

**0 → appear → travel → disappear**

rather than:

**visible → move → reset → visible again**

That is a much cleaner animation lifecycle.

---

# One more thing: the landing position

This is the part I would implement next **before making the electricity pretty**.

We need to tell the `LandingEnergy` shader:

> "The ball landed at X = this."

Then the shader can use something like:

```text
landing_x
```

instead of assuming the effect starts at the left side.

That gives us:

```text
Ball lands
     ↓
landing_x = actual contact position
     ↓
energy originates there
     ↓
propagates across surface
```

And **that** is what will make it feel like a reaction to the landing rather than a generic animation attached to every platform.

---

## So my recommendation

**Don't polish the current wandering-ball effect. Scrap that implementation.**

Keep the `LandingEnergy` node because the separate layer is still the right architecture, but replace its shader logic with:

> **Landing-origin surface propagation field**

Then we'll build the visual in one reasonably large implementation:

1. Pass landing X into `LandingEnergy`
2. Make it completely invisible when idle
3. Create a tiny impact spark at that X
4. Propagate an irregular energy front across the surface
5. Leave a short fading trail behind the front
6. Make the whole thing disappear smoothly
7. Only *then* tune the electricity character

That should get us much closer to the effect you're imagining without falling into another rabbit hole of increasingly complicated shader experiments.

# 2. Replace the LandingEnergy shader completely

Let's throw away the wandering-ball shader.

Use this:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

render_mode unshaded, blend_add;

instance uniform float landing_energy: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
instance uniform float landing_x: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.5;
instance uniform float platform_width = 220.0;

varying float platform_x;
varying float platform_y;

void vertex() {
	platform_x = VERTEX.x;
	platform_y = VERTEX.y;
}

void fragment() {

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// 1. NORMALIZED PLATFORM COORDINATES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float half_width = platform_width * 0.5;

	float x = (
		platform_x + half_width
	) / platform_width;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 2. IDLE = COMPLETELY INVISIBLE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float energy = landing_energy;

	if (energy <= 0.001) {
		COLOR = vec4(0.0);
		return;
	}

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 3. IMPACT PHASE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float impact = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.16,
		energy
	);

	// Quick bright flash at the actual landing point.
	float impact_distance = abs(
		x - landing_x
	);

	float impact_core = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.025,
		impact_distance
	);

	float impact_aura = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.02,
		0.10,
		impact_distance
	);

	float impact_strength =
		impact_core +
		impact_aura * 0.35;

	impact_strength *= impact;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 4. PROPAGATION
	// --------------------------------------------------

	// Wait briefly for the impact before the energy starts
	// travelling.
	float travel_phase = smoothstep(
		0.08,
		0.22,
		energy
	);

	// The front travels from the landing point toward
	// the right side of the platform.
	float travel_distance = 1.25;

	float front_x =
		landing_x +
		travel_phase * travel_distance;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 5. IRREGULAR ELECTRICAL FRONT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float local_distance =
		x - front_x;

	// Wobble the front so it doesn't look like a
	// perfectly straight scanning line.
	float wobble =
		sin(
			x * 42.0 +
			energy * 28.0
		) * 0.018;

	local_distance += wobble;

float front_core = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.018,
		abs(local_distance)
	);

	float front_aura = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.012,
		0.055,
		abs(local_distance)
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 6. SURFACE TRAIL BEHIND THE FRONT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float behind =
		front_x - x;

	float trail = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.02,
		0.24,
		behind
	);

	// Don't allow trail in front of the energy.
	trail *= step(
		0.0,
		behind
	);

	// Trail becomes weaker over distance.
	trail *= 0.28;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 7. SMALL ELECTRICAL BRANCHES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float branch_wave =
		sin(
			x * 75.0 +
			energy * 31.0
		);

	float branch_shape =
		smoothstep(
			0.55,
			0.90,
			branch_wave
		);

	float branch_distance =
		abs(local_distance);

	float branches = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.045,
		branch_distance
	);

	branches *= branch_shape;
	branches *= 0.55;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 8. FADE OUT AT THE END
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float fade = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.78,
		1.0,
		energy
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 9. SURFACE HEIGHT MASK
	// --------------------------------------------------

	// The effect is concentrated around the platform
	// surface rather than filling the entire LandingEnergy
	// rectangle.

	float surface_distance = abs(
		platform_y + 7.0
	);

	float surface_mask = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		2.0,
		15.0,
		surface_distance
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 10. COMBINE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float intensity =
		impact_strength +
		front_core * 1.25 +
		front_aura * 0.35 +
		trail +
		branches;

	intensity *= fade;
	intensity *= surface_mask;

vec3 energy_color = vec3(
		0.0,
		0.85,
		1.0
	);

	COLOR = vec4(
		energy_color * intensity,
		intensity
	);
}
```

This is deliberately **not** trying to make a realistic lightning simulation.

The important visual structure is:

```text
landing point
     ↓
     ✦
─────╲╱────────────────────
       ╲
        ✦─────→
          ·───→
```

The **front** is the important part. The trail and branches are supporting elements.

### 1. Shader `return` error

Godot doesn't allow us to use `return` to exit the `fragment()` processor like that. ([GitHub](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/55234?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So remove this:

```glsl
float energy = landing_energy;

if (energy <= 0.001) {
	COLOR = vec4(0.0);
	return;
}
```

and replace it with:

```glsl
float energy = landing_energy;
```

Then, rather than returning early, we'll make the **entire effect multiply by an activity value**:

```glsl
float active = smoothstep(
	0.0,
	0.02,
	energy
);
```

At `landing_energy = 0`, `active = 0`, so the effect becomes invisible without needing `return`.

At the end, change:

```glsl
intensity *= fade;
intensity *= surface_mask;
```

to:

```glsl
intensity *= fade;
intensity *= surface_mask;
intensity *= active;
```

That's the proper way to handle the idle state here.

---

# 2. And yes - that is the exact call we need to change

You found the only call site:

```gdscript
func _landed_jump_multiplier() -> float:
	for i in get_slide_collision_count():
		var collider: Object = get_slide_collision(i).get_collider()
		if collider is Node and collider.has_method("on_ball_landed"):
			return collider.on_ball_landed()
```

We **don't** need to search elsewhere.

Change it to:

```gdscript
func _landed_jump_multiplier() -> float:
	for i in get_slide_collision_count():
		var collider: Object = get_slide_collision(i).get_collider()

		if collider is Node and collider.has_method("on_ball_landed"):
			return collider.on_ball_landed(global_position.x)

	return 1.0
```

The important addition is:

```gdscript
global_position.x
```

That gives the platform the ball's X position when the collision is detected.

So the flow is now:

```text
Ball
 ↓
collision detected
 ↓
global_position.x
 ↓
Platform.on_ball_landed(ball_x)
 ↓
calculate ball position relative to platform
 ↓
landing_ratio
 ↓
LandingEnergy.landing_x
 ↓
impact exactly where the ball landed
```

That's the connection we were missing.

### One thing I want you to check

Your `_landed_jump_multiplier()` currently has no explicit:

```gdscript
return 1.0
```

after the loop.

**Add it.** Otherwise the function can fall through without returning a value if no suitable collider is found.

So use exactly:

```gdscript
func _landed_jump_multiplier() -> float:
	for i in get_slide_collision_count():
		var collider: Object = get_slide_collision(i).get_collider()

		if collider is Node and collider.has_method("on_ball_landed"):
			return collider.on_ball_landed(global_position.x)

	return 1.0
```

Everything else from the previous implementation can stay as we had it.

The shader fix is also safe because the effect will now be controlled by `active` instead of trying to exit `fragment()`. Godot's shader language supports runtime `if`, but `fragment()` is a processor function and using `return` there is not the right pattern for this case. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/shading_language.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Yeah - **seeing your concept makes the missing piece much clearer.**

The current `LandingEnergy` isn't really reading as a landing impact. It's reading as **“a glowing thing moves along the platform.”** That is why it feels like random debris even though the shader itself is working.

And I agree with your instinct: **we should not just polish that into a prettier wandering fragment.** The landing should have an actual impact event first, with the surface-traveling energy becoming a secondary continuation of that impact.

### What your concept is doing right

Looking at the platform with the ball on it, there are really **three visual layers**:

1. **A soft expanding impact aura/ring**
   
   The landing point gets a circular/elliptical glow that expands outward and quickly fades.

2. **A compact burst**
   
   A handful of little particles/sparks shoot outward from the landing point. They're sparse, not a particle explosion.

3. **Energy streaks / filaments**
   
   Several thin glowing lines shoot outward from the contact point, giving the feeling that the platform itself received an energy impulse.

Then, underneath all of that, the platform can have the **surface energy propagation** we've already started.

That's much closer to a believable game landing effect.

---

## And yes: shader can do most of this

A CanvasItem shader is absolutely capable of generating things like the expanding ring, soft aura, directional streaks and radial energy lines. CanvasItem shaders operate directly on the 2D geometry and support additive blending, so this type of effect is a good fit. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/canvas_item_shader.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

But I **wouldn't force everything into one shader**.

For the little particles, Godot's `GPUParticles2D` is specifically designed for effects such as sparks and other small bursts, supports one-shot emission, lifetime, randomness, etc. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_gpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

So I'd build the landing effect like this:

```text
Platform
├── CollisionShape2D
├── Visual
├── NeonEdge
├── LandingEnergy
├── LandingImpact
└── LandingParticles
```

### `LandingImpact`
Shader-based.

Handles:

- soft ring
- impact aura
- radial energy lines
- tiny directional streaks

### `LandingParticles`
`GPUParticles2D`.

Handles:

- ~5-10 tiny sparks
- very short lifetime
- low spread
- slight randomness
- fading quickly

### `LandingEnergy`
Our existing surface effect.

Handles:

- energy traveling across the platform surface
- **but now in both directions**

And that's the important part for your left/right problem.

---

# 1. The energy should NOT always travel left → right

You're absolutely right about this.

Current behavior:

```text
LAND LEFT
●──────────────→

LAND RIGHT
              ●
              →    (almost no room)
```

That's inherently dependent on where you land.

Instead:

```text
LAND LEFT

●──────→
╰────→

LAND CENTER

←────●────→

LAND RIGHT

        ←────●
          ←──╯
```

So the landing creates **two surface waves**, one going left and one going right.

They both originate from:

```gdscript
landing_ratio
```

and move toward the platform edges.

That also means the effect naturally looks different depending on where you land, which is actually desirable.

A landing near the left edge produces a short left wave + a long right wave.

A landing in the center produces two balanced waves.

A landing near the right edge produces a long left wave + short right wave.

**That feels physically connected to the impact point instead of looking like a preset animation.**

---

# 2. I'd make the energy slower and larger

I agree with you here too.

Right now:

> tiny → fast → disappears → "what was that?"

We want more like:

> impact → energy catches → travels → dissipates

I'd roughly target:

```text
0.00s   impact
0.05s   surface energy appears
0.15s   starts traveling
0.55s   still clearly visible
0.80s   fades out
```

Not a huge slow effect.

Just enough that your eye actually gets to **follow it**.

And the surface energy should probably be **wider/stronger**, not necessarily dramatically brighter.

That's important.

Instead of:

```text
tiny bright pixel
```

we want something closer to:

```text
━━━━━ glowing filament ━━━━━
```

with a soft halo around it.

---

# 3. Same color as the landing edge - YES

I would absolutely synchronize these.

Your concept uses a cohesive energy language, and your game already has:

```text
Normal:
cyan neon edge
```

then on landing:

```text
landing:
energized cyan/blue edge
```

So all landing energy should use that **same landing color**.

Something like:

```gdscript
LANDING_EDGE_COLOR
```

should drive:

- NeonEdge
- LandingImpact
- LandingEnergy
- LandingParticles

That way you don't get:

```text
edge = blue
surface = cyan
particles = turquoise
ring = white
```

which starts looking like several unrelated effects.

Instead:

```text
               SAME ENERGY
                    ↓
       ┌────────────┴────────────┐
       ↓                         ↓
  landing edge              impact system
                                  ↓
                         ┌────────┼────────┐
                         ↓        ↓        ↓
                       aura    lines    particles
                                  ↓
                          surface energy
```

We can still use different **intensity** and transparency per layer without changing the hue.

---

# 4. The shockwave is the real missing ingredient

This is the biggest thing I'd change.

When the ball hits, there should be a very short visual:

```text
       ╭────────╮
      ╱          ╲
     │     ●      │
      ╲          ╱
       ╰────────╯
```

But because your platform is only 20 px high, I **wouldn't make it a perfect giant circle**.

I'd make it more like a horizontally compressed energy shockwave:

```text
              ╭───────╮
           ╭──╯       ╰──╮
───────────●───────────────
           ╰──╮       ╭──╯
              ╰───────╯
```

Very fast expansion.

Very soft.

Then it disappears.

The eye reads:

**impact → force radiates outward.**

That one thing will make the landing feel substantially more physical.

---

# 5. The radial energy lines from your concept are also worth keeping

This part is especially nice:

```text
          ╱
        ╱
───────●───────
      ╲
       ╲
```

Not dozens of lines.

Maybe **4-7 tiny energy filaments**, each with:

- different length
- slightly different angle
- slightly different delay
- quick fade

That gives us the "energy burst" appearance without turning it into fireworks.

And because the lines originate at the actual `landing_x`, the effect will always feel attached to the ball.

---

# 6. The particles should be VERY restrained

I wouldn't make it:

```text
💥💥💥💥💥💥💥
```

More like:

```text
        ·
    ·
      ╲
──────●──────
   ·       ·
```

Maybe 6-8 particles total.

Some slightly upward.

Some almost horizontal.

A couple tiny glowing dots.

Short lifetime.

Then gone.

Godot's `GPUParticles2D` supports one-shot emission specifically for this kind of event, so we can trigger a compact burst on each landing rather than running a permanent particle system. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_gpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

---

# So I would NOT throw away `LandingEnergy`

I'd change its role.

Right now you're basically asking it to do:

> "be the landing effect."

That's too much.

Instead:

### `LandingImpact`
**The landing.**

Fast:

```text
impact
↓
ring
↓
burst
↓
fade
```

### `LandingParticles`
**Physical detail.**

```text
spark spark spark
```

### `LandingEnergy`
**The energy left behind.**

```text
<──────●──────>
        ↓
    travels outward
```

That hierarchy makes much more sense visually.

---

# And the coolest part

This means we can make the whole thing happen from **one landing position**:

```gdscript
on_ball_landed(global_position.x)
```

which we're already changing the API to support.

Then:

```text
landing_x
    │
    ├──► NeonEdge pulse
    │
    ├──► Impact shockwave center
    │
    ├──► Radial energy burst origin
    │
    ├──► Particle emitter position
    │
    └──► Surface energy origin
```

So there is one physical event, and every visual component responds to that same event.

**That's what will make it feel like one effect rather than five effects stacked on top of each other.**

---

## My recommendation for the final landing sequence

Something around:

```text
0.00
BALL CONTACT
│
├─ edge flashes
├─ body illuminates
├─ soft shockwave appears
├─ 5-8 sparks burst outward
└─ radial energy filaments shoot out
│

```

That gives us the exact feeling you're describing:

**impact first → energy burst → energy propagation.**

Not:

**tiny blue object wandering around after the ball touches the platform.** 💀

And importantly, we don't need to turn this into some gigantic VFX system. **One CanvasItem shader for the impact + one tiny GPUParticles2D burst + our surface shader** is enough to get very close to the concept.

I think **this is the direction we should implement now**, rather than spending more time polishing the current one-way traveling fragment.

	Vector2(-hw, energy_bottom)
])

_landing_energy.color = Color.WHITE
```

with:

```gdscript
var energy_height := 34.0
var energy_top := -hh - energy_height
var energy_bottom := -hh + 5.0

_landing_energy.polygon = PackedVector2Array([
	Vector2(-hw, energy_top),
	Vector2(hw, energy_top),
	Vector2(hw, energy_bottom),
	Vector2(-hw, energy_bottom)
])

_landing_energy.color = Color.WHITE

_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
	"platform_width",
	width * width_scale
)

_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
	"surface_y",
	-hh
)

_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(

	LANDING_EDGE_COLOR

The extra height gives the shockwave some actual room to exist above the platform.

# 3. Replace the ENTIRE `platform_landing_surface.gdshader`

We're going to completely replace the current one-way propagation shader.

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

render_mode unshaded, blend_add;

instance uniform float landing_energy: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
instance uniform float landing_x: hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.5;

instance uniform float platform_width = 220.0;
instance uniform float surface_y = -10.0;

instance uniform vec4 landing_color : source_color = vec4(0.12, 0.32, 1.0, 1.0);

varying float platform_x;
varying float platform_y;

void vertex() {
	platform_x = VERTEX.x;
	platform_y = VERTEX.y;
}

float segment_distance(
	vec2 p,
	vec2 a,
	vec2 b
) {
	vec2 ab = b - a;

	float t = dot(
		p - a,
		ab
	) / max(dot(ab, ab), 0.0001);

	t = clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0);

	vec2 closest = a + ab * t;

	return distance(
		p,
		closest
	);
}

void fragment() {

	// --------------------------------------------------
	// 1. BASIC COORDINATES
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float half_width = platform_width * 0.5;

	float impact_x = mix(
		-half_width,
		half_width,
		landing_x
	);

	vec2 p = vec2(
		platform_x,
		platform_y
	);

	vec2 impact_point = vec2(
		impact_x,
		surface_y
	);

	float energy = landing_energy;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 2. GLOBAL ACTIVITY
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float active = smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.015,
		energy
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 3. IMPACT BURST
	// --------------------------------------------------

	// The first ~20% of the animation is the actual hit.

	float impact_phase = smoothstep(
		0.0,
		0.20,
		energy
	);

	float impact_fade = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.12,
		0.30,
		energy
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 4. EXPANDING SHOCKWAVE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	vec2 shock_scale = vec2(
		0.42,
		1.0
	);

	float shock_distance = length(
		(p - impact_point) * shock_scale
	);

	float shock_radius = mix(
		2.0,
		42.0,
		impact_phase
	);

	float shock_ring = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		5.5,
		abs(
			shock_distance - shock_radius
		)
	);

	// Soft glow surrounding the ring.
	float shock_aura = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		9.0,
		abs(
			shock_distance - shock_radius
		)
	);

	shock_ring *= impact_fade;
	shock_aura *= impact_fade * 0.35;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 5. CENTRAL LANDING FLASH
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float impact_distance = distance(
		p,
		impact_point
	);

	float impact_core = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		2.0,
		8.0,
		impact_distance
	);

	impact_core *= impact_fade;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 6. RADIAL ENERGY STREAKS
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float streak_energy = 0.0;

	streak_energy += 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		4.0,
		segment_distance(
			p,
			impact_point,
			impact_point + vec2(-42.0, -16.0)
		)
	);

	streak_energy += 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		4.0,
		segment_distance(
			p,
			impact_point,
			impact_point + vec2(-22.0, -27.0)
		)
	);

	streak_energy += 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		4.0,
		segment_distance(
			p,
			impact_point,
			impact_point + vec2(8.0, -31.0)
		)
	);

	streak_energy += 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		4.0,
		segment_distance(
			p,
			impact_point,
			impact_point + vec2(30.0, -23.0)
		)
	);

	streak_energy += 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.5,
		4.0,
		segment_distance(
			p,
			impact_point,
			impact_point + vec2(48.0, -10.0)
		)
	);

	streak_energy *= impact_fade;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 7. TWO-WAY SURFACE PROPAGATION
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float travel_phase = smoothstep(
		0.16,
		0.95,
		energy
	);

	float travel_distance = platform_width * 0.60;

	float left_front =
		impact_x -
		travel_phase * travel_distance;

	float right_front =
		impact_x +
		travel_phase * travel_distance;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 8. SMALL FRONT WOBBLE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float wobble =
		sin(
			platform_x * 0.12 +
			energy * 18.0
		) * 2.0;

float left_distance =
		abs(
			platform_x -
			(left_front + wobble)
		);

	float right_distance =
		abs(
			platform_x -
			(right_front - wobble)
		);

float left_front_energy = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		5.0,
		left_distance
	);

	float right_front_energy = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.0,
		5.0,
		right_distance
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 9. SURFACE TRAILS
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float left_trail_distance =
		impact_x - platform_x;

	float right_trail_distance =
		platform_x - impact_x;

float left_trail = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		4.0,
		42.0,
		abs(
			left_trail_distance -
			travel_phase * travel_distance
		)
	);

	float right_trail = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		4.0,
		42.0,
		abs(
			right_trail_distance -
			travel_phase * travel_distance
		)
	);

	float surface_energy =
		left_front_energy +
		right_front_energy +
		(left_trail + right_trail) * 0.18;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 10. SURFACE MASK
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float surface_distance =
		abs(
			platform_y - surface_y
		);

	float surface_mask = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		1.0,
		13.0,
		surface_distance
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 11. OVERALL FADE
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float fade = 1.0 - smoothstep(
		0.78,
		1.0,
		energy
	);

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 12. COMBINE IMPACT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float impact_effect =
		shock_ring * 1.25 +
		shock_aura +
		impact_core * 1.4 +
		streak_energy * 0.55;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 13. COMBINE SURFACE ENERGY
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float surface_effect =
		surface_energy * surface_mask;

float intensity =
		impact_effect +
		surface_effect;

intensity *= fade;
	intensity *= active;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// 14. OUTPUT
	// --------------------------------------------------

	vec3 final_color =
		landing_color.rgb *
		intensity;

	COLOR = vec4(
		final_color,
		intensity
	);
}
```

### What this changes visually

The old effect:

```text
●──────────────→
```

is gone.

The new effect has:

```text
           ╱│╲
        ╱   │   ╲
───────●────┼────────
      ╲     │    ╱
        ╲───┴──╱
        ←     →
```

followed by:

```text
────────←────●────→────────
```

So **landing near the right edge is no longer a dead effect**. You'll get a large left-going propagation and a short right-going one.

---

# 4. Make the surface energy slower

Your current tween is:

```gdscript
0.0,
1.0,
0.80
```

Change that to:

```gdscript
0.0,
1.0,
1.05
```

So:

```gdscript
tween.tween_method(
	func(value: float) -> void:
		_landing_energy.set_instance_shader_parameter(
			"landing_energy",
			value
		),
	0.0,
	1.0,
	1.05
).set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUAD).set_ease(Tween.EASE_IN_OUT)
```

This is intentionally only a modest increase. I don't want the energy crawling across the platform; we just need enough time for the eye to register the propagation.

---

# 5. One important thing we're deliberately NOT doing yet

I'm **not adding the actual GPUParticles2D burst in this pass**.

Not because it isn't possible - it absolutely is, and Godot's particle system is suitable for one-shot sparks. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/2d/particle_systems_2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

I want to see the new:

**impact ring + radial energy streaks + two-way surface propagation**

first.

Because if this already gives us:

> **LAND → BOOM → energy radiates → travels across surface**

then we only need a tiny particle layer to add physical detail.

If it doesn't, we'll know exactly what needs changing without simultaneously debugging a particle system.

---

### One more important detail

We're deliberately using the same:

```gdscript
LANDING_EDGE_COLOR
```

for the shader through:

```gdscript
"landing_color"
```

So your `#1F51FF` test color is now the **actual energy language** of the entire impact.

And because `LandingEnergy` is still a `Polygon2D` with a ShaderMaterial, this doesn't require a texture; `Polygon2D` supports custom materials and shader-driven rendering directly. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.4/classes/class_polygon2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

**I would run this exact version before changing anything else.** The important test isn't "is every streak beautiful?" - it's whether the landing now reads immediately as **impact → energy burst → surface propagation** rather than "random glowing object moving around."

---

**Sources:**

- [2D particle systems — Godot Engine (latest) documentation in English](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/2d/particle_systems_2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Yes - I think we're at the point where **the basic idea is correct, but the effect needs to be designed as an actual impact effect rather than a single shader doing everything in the same shape**.

And the problems you noticed all make sense:

- **Cut off:** the `LandingEnergy` Polygon2D is physically too small for the shockwave/streaks. A CanvasItem shader cannot draw outside its CanvasItem's geometry. - **Randomness:** absolutely possible. We can give every landing a random seed through an `instance uniform`, which Godot supports for CanvasItems. ([GitHub](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-docs/blob/master/classes/class_canvasitem.rst?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

## 1. Replace `platform_landing_surface.gdshader`

**Streaks**

- different lengths
- different angles
- different widths
- don't all terminate at the same radius
- some are short, some longer
- deliberately stronger than now

**Surface propagation**
- travels **left + right**
- still originates from landing point
- has a slightly irregular front
- remains much flatter than the impact

**Randomness**
- every landing gets a new `effect_seed`
- ring size/thickness
- streak lengths
- streak positions
- streak angles

instance uniform vec4 landing_color : source_color =
	vec4(0.12, 0.32, 1.0, 1.0);

varying float platform_x;
varying float platform_y;

	platform_y = VERTEX.y;

// --------------------------------------------------
// RANDOM

float random_float(float value) {

// --------------------------------------------------

float ring(

		platform_x -
		impact_x;

		1.0 -
		smoothstep(
			4.0,
			38.0,
			abs(
				left_distance -
				travel_phase *

	float right_trail =
		1.0 -
		smoothstep(
			4.0,
			38.0,
			abs(
				right_distance -
				travel_phase *
				travel_distance
			)
		);

float surface_energy =
		left_front_energy +
		right_front_energy +
		(left_trail + right_trail) * 0.20;

// --------------------------------------------------
	// SURFACE MASK
	// --------------------------------------------------

	float surface_distance =
		abs(
			platform_y -
			surface_y
		);

	float surface_mask =
		1.0 -
		smoothstep(
			1.0,
			11.0,

		);

		landing_color.rgb *

([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/classes/class_particleprocessmaterial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

	LANDING_EDGE_COLOR
)

add:

)

```text

Impact aura appears
 ↓
6-9 randomized energy streaks burst outward

```
