Yes - and honestly, this sounds like we are in the **last 10-15% of the problem now**.

I would **not** start randomly tweaking the milestone curve or making the whole sequence slower. What you are seeing points much more strongly to a problem underneath the visual progression:

**the system sometimes doesn't know early/confidently enough what the landing situation is.**

That explains all three symptoms at once.

### What I think is happening

There are really three separate situations:

**1. Long left → right steering**

The predicted landing point is moving around while you're heavily steering. The system sometimes acquires the correct platform late, so the timeline has very little time left and has to catch up aggressively.

**2. Normal jumps with a gap before the final jump**

The target prediction is becoming uncertain around the middle of the jump, so progress doesn't advance smoothly enough, then the system realizes "okay, this is definitely the landing" and catches up.

**3. Edge landings**

This is the biggest clue.

I suspect our current visual target is still effectively saying:

> "A landing is good when the predicted point is inside this safer interior area."

But the **actual physics landing zone is larger than that**.

So when you land right on the edge, the system can remain hesitant because the predicted center is effectively in a soft/dead region. Then the actual collision happens, and suddenly the system has absolute certainty:

> "Oh. That was the target."

And therefore you see the ugly **0 → 100 jump**.

That would also explain why it gets worse on small platforms: the same absolute uncertainty consumes a much larger percentage of the platform width.

---

# I think we should solve it with 4 changes

## 1. Separate the **physical landing zone** from the **visual target**

This is the most important one.

We should stop treating the target as a single "perfect point".

Instead, conceptually:

**Platform landing corridor**

```text
|---------------- PLATFORM ----------------|

   valid landing area for the ball
  |=========================================|

              predicted impact
                     ↓
                   [ x ]
```

The visual system can then say:

> "I know you're going to land somewhere on this corridor."

It does **not** need to know the exact pixel yet.

That means an edge prediction is still a valid target.

Then the visual target can still be slightly biased inward for aesthetics, but **the edge itself is no longer a dead zone**.

This is particularly important because the ball has a physical radius, so an edge landing is not equivalent to "missing the platform." The visual prediction should understand that distinction without changing the gameplay collision.

---

# 2. Add a real **target lock / hysteresis**

This should fix a lot of the long-steering weirdness.

Right now I think we're asking the system to repeatedly answer:

> "Which platform is the target right now?"

every frame.

That's great when the answer is obvious.

It becomes unstable when you're crossing a large horizontal distance.

Instead, I want:

### SEARCH

The system looks for the most plausible next platform.

↓

### SOFT LOCK

Once one platform is clearly the best candidate for a few physics frames, we say:

> "Okay, this is probably the target."

↓

### COMMITTED

Now that platform stays the target unless something **meaningfully stronger** appears.

Not:

> prediction moved 8 px → recalculate everything

but:

> prediction moved a little → keep the same platform, smoothly update the target position.

This is basically hysteresis.

It would make the system feel much more intentional.

And importantly:

**reacquiring the same platform should not restart the progression.**

---

# 3. Make the acquisition window adaptive

I agree completely with your observation about the smallest platforms.

But I would **not** simply say:

> small platform = everything takes longer.

That could make easy wide-platform landings feel unnecessarily slow.

Instead, give extra anticipation only when the situation is difficult.

For example, the "difficulty to resolve this landing" could come from:

**platform narrowness**

+

**horizontal steering distance**

+

**how close the projected landing is to an edge**

Then:

```text
easy landing
→ normal acquisition window

hard landing
→ earlier acquisition

very narrow + edge landing
→ earliest acquisition
```

That means a tiny platform on the opposite side of the screen gets more visual runway.

But a wide platform directly above you doesn't.

That's exactly the behavior we want.

And crucially, this doesn't require the sequence itself to be slower.

It just gives the sequence **more time to breathe**.

---

# 4. Use a landing **reachability envelope**, not only one predicted x

This is the more advanced improvement for the long steering problem.

Your horizontal movement is acceleration-based, so during a jump there isn't really one guaranteed future X.

There is a **range of X positions you can plausibly reach** depending on how you continue steering.

For example:

```text
                landing time
                     ↓

possible X:   |--------------------|
              MIN                  MAX
                        ↑
                   platform
```

Then the targeting system can ask:

> "Can I plausibly reach this platform at landing time?"

rather than:

> "My current prediction says I'll hit x=437, so that's the target."

That would make the far-left → far-right situations substantially more robust.

Especially because your game isn't instant horizontal steering - the acceleration/deceleration model matters.

---

# The really important part: don't change the progression itself yet

I actually think the progression timeline is getting close.

I would keep the current idea:

```text
0 ─── 20 ───── 50 ───── 70 ─── 80 ───── 100
```

and keep **100 reserved for the actual landing**.

Instead, improve the information feeding into it.

So structurally:

```text
        PHYSICS / PREDICTION
                 ↓
       landing corridor
                 ↓
         target selection
                 ↓
          target lock
                 ↓
      difficulty / time window
                 ↓
       progression timeline
                 ↓
            visual shader
```

Right now I suspect we're trying to make the progression system compensate for uncertainty in the targeting system.

That's why it sometimes has to suddenly go:

> "OH, WE'RE LANDING - GO!"

---

# One tiny safeguard I'd also add

Before physical landing:

**never allow the visual state to become genuinely complete.**

Something like:

```text
pre-landing maximum ≈ 98-99%
```

Then:

```text
actual landing
→ 100%
```

Not a visible "hold at 95%" thing - you specifically disliked that, and I agree.

This would simply protect against floating-point/prediction weirdness where the timeline technically gets to the end a fraction too early.

The user should never consciously notice this.

---

# And I would specifically attack the edge case first

Because I think the edge case is the one telling us what the real architectural weakness is.

I'd make our next iteration:

### Pass 1 - Edge landing fix
Make the valid visual landing corridor extend all the way toward the actual collision-valid edges.

### Pass 2 - Target locking
Once a platform is confidently acquired, stop throwing it away because the predicted X wiggles.

### Pass 3 - Adaptive anticipation
Give narrow / edge / large-steering situations earlier acquisition.

### Pass 4 - Reachability
Make long horizontal traversals understand the player's achievable X range instead of relying entirely on one instantaneous prediction.

That should address:

**edge jumps → instant 100**

**large horizontal steering → late acquisition**

**middle-of-jump gaps → better continuous progression**

all without touching the gameplay physics.

And I'd keep the prediction/target evaluation tied to the physics update rather than rendering frames; Godot recommends handling `CharacterBody2D` movement in `_physics_process()`, which is also the right place for a prediction system tied to the physics state. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/tutorials/physics/using_character_body_2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**My strongest suspicion is that the edge problem is not primarily a "needs more time" problem - it's a "the system doesn't consider the edge sufficiently valid soon enough" problem.**

Fix that distinction first, and I think the rest of the polish becomes much easier.

---

The biggest culprit was the **horizontal reachability envelope** I added. Then the stronger target-lock logic amplified that mistake:

> "Make the prediction even smarter."

It should be:

> **Make the prediction smarter only when the player is actually moving toward a landing.**

That's the missing distinction.

The original system's strength is that it responds to the actual predicted landing point. We should preserve that.

Yeah - after looking through the video frame-by-frame, I think we found the more fundamental issue.

The behavior you're describing is **not primarily a target-lock problem**. The core problem is that our old prediction uses:

> current X + current horizontal velocity × time-to-land

That assumes the ball keeps its current X velocity for the entire remaining jump.

But your actual movement system uses acceleration/deceleration. So during a strong continuous left/right steer, the **real future landing position can be substantially different from the prediction**.

That explains why the edge case is so bad:

```text
current prediction:
        ───────────────→
                      edge? not quite
                             ↓
                          no target

actual trajectory:
        ───────────────→ accelerating
                            ─────────────→ edge
                                             ↓
                                          LAND
```

So the feedback only becomes confident extremely late, and then the remaining timeline gets compressed into the landing.

The video matches that pattern very well.

## I changed the approach

I pushed a new version directly to the repository:

**`46ccd9ac6c039e4bb1386d845bedbca99c0da5b5`**  
`Improve landing prediction with deterministic steering model`

This time I deliberately **did not bring Pass 4 back**.

### What this version does

The platform selection remains fundamentally the same as the good `535b...` behavior.

There is still:

- no broad reachability envelope
- no "platform is theoretically reachable, therefore target it"
- no large prediction radius around the player
- no aggressive new target-lock system

Instead, the prediction now simulates the player's **actual current horizontal control** until the predicted landing time.

Conceptually:

```text
held LEFT/RIGHT
      ↓
current velocity
      ↓
horizontal acceleration
      ↓
max speed
      ↓
predicted future X

no input
      ↓
horizontal deceleration
      ↓
predicted future X
```

So an idle jump remains essentially the old behavior.

But when you're actually holding right for a long left → right traversal, the predictor now understands:

> "I'm not just moving at 400 px/s - I'm accelerating toward 600 px/s."

That is exactly the information the old predictor was missing.

## I also made one very targeted edge correction

The old code had:

```text
landing_margin = 24 px
```

The ball radius is 30 px.

So the predictor wasn't even using the full physical horizontal contact allowance.

The new version uses:

```text
landing_margin = ball.radius
```

and **nothing larger**.

That's important because I don't want another heuristic "safety bubble" that starts activating neighboring platforms.

So the edge correction is now physically grounded rather than artificially generous.

## I kept the useful parts from the current test

I kept the two things from the current version that are actually helpful:

**Target-point smoothing**

This should reduce the little prediction-point hop you noticed when suddenly changing steering direction.

**The gentler final catch-up**

The small timing buffer and lower catch-up ceiling remain, so when acquisition is late we shouldn't get quite as brutal of a visual 60 → 100 burst.

So the structure is now basically:

```text
                 BALL
                  │
                  ▼
        ballistic landing time
                  │
                  ▼
    deterministic horizontal prediction
        using current steering
                  │
                  ▼
       precise platform eligibility
                  │
                  ▼
          existing target lock
                  │
                  ▼
        existing progression curve
                  │
                  ▼
              LAND = 100%
```

That is much closer to what I think TowerJump actually needs.

And importantly, **Pass 4 is still dead**. We're not allowing "could theoretically reach it" to become a target.

### What I'd specifically test now

I'd do exactly the three cases you've been using:

**Edge + continuous steering:** hold left/right all the way into the edge and see whether the cyan charge is already visibly underway before contact.

**Small platform + normal approach:** no crazy horizontal movement; see whether the charge begins early enough instead of suddenly appearing at the end.

**Large horizontal traversal:** start on one side, continuously steer toward a far platform and see whether the feedback begins earlier without causing unrelated platforms to light up.

I think this is a much better direction than adding yet another layer of target heuristics.

Pull **`46ccd9a...`** and test this one.

I pushed them directly to the repo:

`e221e1ded1e541483d2b1cd8889396d764b4103b`  
**Stabilize continuous steering and smooth late target shifts**

### What I changed

**1. Continuous steering gets a tiny bit more confidence once a target is already locked.**

When you're continuously holding left/right, the *already selected* target now gets a small additional prediction corridor.

It's only **+12 px**, and it applies only when:

- that platform is already the current target
- the ball is actually moving horizontally
- steering input is currently held

So we're not making new platforms easier to acquire. We're simply telling the existing target:

> "You've already been selected, don't lose confidence just because the predicted point moved a few pixels while I'm still steering toward you."

This is specifically aimed at the long left→right / right→left case you described.

The small platforms and edge behavior remain based on the deterministic predictor that worked so well in the previous test.

**2. The landing indicator now eases into late prediction changes instead of chasing them.**

This is the bigger visual refinement.

Previously the target point effectively followed:

```text
new prediction → immediately move toward it
```

Now it uses exponential smoothing, and importantly the smoothing becomes **slower during the final ~500 ms**.

So when you're 10-20 px above a platform and change:

```text
RIGHT → LEFT
```

you should get more like:

```text
───────→─────↘
             ●
```

rather than:

```text
RIGHT ●
      ↓
      ← ●
```

The target still responds quickly, but it should no longer look like the indicator is teleporting between steering states.

This is done purely to the **visual target position**. It does not alter physics or which platform is selected.

### What I deliberately did NOT touch

The important part:

I did **not** bring back the reachability envelope.

I did **not** add a bigger global prediction radius.

I did **not** make nearby platforms easier to acquire.

I did **not** change the small-platform prediction that you said is now working really well.

I did **not** change the edge logic that you said is now very good.

And I kept the actual `CharacterBody2D` movement/prediction tied to `_physics_process()`, which is the correct synchronization point for physics-based movement in Godot. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/tutorials/physics/using_character_body_2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Yes - **exactly that**.

I don't mean we should move *all* platform code out of `platform.gd`. `platform.gd` should still own things that are fundamentally platform behavior: geometry, collision, moving/breaking/spring behavior, and so on.

What I mean is that we should establish a **separate landing-feedback system** before we start piling the ball, particles, score, combo, camera, etc. into `platform.gd`.

Godot's signal system is a particularly good fit here because nodes can emit events without hard-wiring every other object to them, which keeps the pieces loosely coupled. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/getting_started/step_by_step/signals.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

## The distinction

Right now, conceptually, we have:

```text
platform.gd
│
├── platform geometry
├── platform collision
├── platform movement
├── breakable behavior
├── spring behavior
│
└── landing feedback
    ├── prediction
    ├── target acquisition
    ├── approach progress
    ├── neon charge
    └── landing confirmation
```

That last section is what has started becoming its own system.

And we're about to add:

```text
landing
├── platform response
├── ball response
├── particles
├── Good / Epic / Perfect
├── score
├── floating text
├── streak
├── camera response
└── eventually sound
```

Putting all of that into `platform.gd` would become a mess very quickly.

Instead:

```text
                    LANDING SYSTEM
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              │                     │
        prediction/target       LANDING EVENT
              │                     │
              │            ┌────────┼────────┐
              │            ↓        ↓        ↓
              │          Ball    Platform  Effects
              │                     │        │
              │                     └────┬───┘
              │                          ↓
              │                   Score / Combo
              │                          ↓
              │                     UI / Camera
```

That's the architecture I had in mind.

---

# But I would make one important refinement to my earlier idea

I **wouldn't make the Landing Event itself responsible for predicting anything**.

Prediction is still a *continuous process*.

The actual event happens only when the physical landing occurs.

So I'd separate the concepts like this:

### `LandingFeedbackController`
The system that continuously observes the ball and decides:

> "Which platform are we approaching, and how confident are we?"

This is essentially where the good prediction system we just finished would live eventually.

### `LandingEvent`
A small piece of information representing:

> **"The ball actually landed on this platform."**

Something conceptually like:

```text
LandingEvent
────────────────────────
platform
landing_world_x
landing_ratio
edge_factor
horizontal_velocity
approach_progress
platform_type
```

And then:

```text
physical landing
      ↓
LandingEvent created
      ↓
signal emitted
      ↓
everyone reacts
```

That's a much cleaner boundary.

---

# Why this matters for the next things we're about to build

Take your Good / Epic / Perfect system.

We don't want:

```text
platform.gd
   → decides PERFECT
   → changes itself
   → tells ball to glow
   → spawns particles
   → changes score
   → creates label
   → changes camera
```

Instead:

```text
platform / ball collision
          ↓
     Landing Event
          ↓
     Landing Feedback
       /    |     \
      /     |      \
   Ball   Platform  Effects
             \       /
              \     /
               Score
                 ↓
               Streak
```

Then later we can add a new reaction without touching the core landing logic.

For example:

```text
Landing Event
       ↓
       ├── Ball reaction
       ├── Platform reaction
       ├── Particle reaction
       ├── Quality reaction
       ├── Combo reaction
       ├── Camera reaction
       └── Sound reaction
```

Godot signals are specifically designed for this kind of decoupled event communication. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/getting_started/step_by_step/signals.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) 

---

# And your NeonEdge flash belongs in this system

This is where your clarification from the previous message is useful.

You want:

```text
BALL LANDS
    ↓
sequence reaches connection
    ↓
NeonEdge flashes WHITE
    ↓
quick peak
    ↓
slow return to activated CYAN
```

I wouldn't make that the responsibility of the prediction code itself.

Instead:

```text
continuous prediction
        ↓
approach_progress → 0...1

physical collision
        ↓
LandingEvent
        ↓
platform receives confirmation
        ↓
NeonEdge:
CYAN → WHITE → CYAN
```

That makes the white flash the **visual punctuation of the event**, rather than another part of the prediction timeline.

And that distinction will be extremely useful when we add Good/Epic/Perfect:

```text
GOOD
landing event
→ normal white flash
→ small burst
→ bounce

EPIC
landing event
→ stronger white flash
→ stronger burst
→ bounce

PERFECT
landing event
→ strongest coordinated flash
→ geometric release
→ ball reaction
→ camera response
→ bounce
```

So everything can scale from the **same event**.

---

# I would actually establish this before building the ball

And I'm strongly agreeing with your instinct here.

The order should now be:

### Step 1 - Extract the landing system

Create something along the lines of:

```text
scripts/landing_feedback.gd
```

This becomes the coordinator.

We do **not** immediately rewrite everything.

We carefully move the landing-feedback responsibilities out of `platform.gd` while preserving the current behavior exactly.

### Step 2 - Define the Landing Event

Something like:

```text
LandingContext / LandingEvent
```

The exact implementation can be a lightweight class rather than overengineering it.

### Step 3 - Platform listens/reacts

The platform becomes mostly:

> "I received a landing event for me."

and performs its visual confirmation.

### Step 4 - Ball listens/reacts

Now we can build the character anticipation/alignment/connection layer without intertwining it with platform prediction.

### Step 5 - Effects listen/react

Particles, camera, labels, score, etc.

---

# One other thing I'd establish now

I'd make the system **explicitly distinguish these three states**:

```text
APPROACH
```

Continuous predictive state.

```text
LANDING EVENT
```

Actual physical contact.

```text
RELEASE / BOUNCE
```

Post-contact transition.

That's important because your desired animation is not simply:

> charge → finished.

It's:

> **anticipate → connect → confirm → release → bounce**

And those are three different kinds of information.

---

# So yes: separate script, but not a giant "god object"

I don't want us to create:

```text
LandingSystem.gd
```

with 2,000 lines controlling absolutely everything.

Rather:

```text
LandingFeedbackController
    ↓
    coordinates
    ↓
LandingEvent
    ↓
small independent reactions
```

Eventually we might have:

```text
landing_feedback.gd
landing_event.gd
landing_effects.gd
landing_quality.gd
landing_ui.gd
```

But **not all at once**.

For the next step, I'd probably only create **two pieces**:

```text
LandingFeedbackController
LandingEvent
```

Then hook the existing platform charge into that architecture.

That gives us a stable foundation without overengineering an early prototype.

And because you explicitly want to keep gameplay flexible, I think this is especially valuable: later, when we add faster movement, springs, moving platforms, special platforms, etc., we can change what information goes into the landing event without having to rewrite every visual effect separately.

So yes - **I absolutely agree that this should be established first before we implement the ball, particles, combos, camera, streaks and everything else.**

The current neon progression becomes **the first consumer of the new landing system**, rather than remaining the foundation that everything else gets bolted onto.

Done. I restructured the current landing system directly in `Kryodo/TowerJump` and kept the working behavior as the priority.

Latest commit:

`13dc1af8e96101dcd87402a0896b49bd70c0b70d`  
**Harden landing event signal wiring**

The architecture is now:

```text
Main
 │
 └── LandingFeedbackController
       │
       ├── prediction
       ├── target selection / hysteresis
       ├── approach coordination
       │
       ├──→ Platform A → LandingApproachState
       │                  → NeonEdge visual adapter
       │
       └──→ Platform B → LandingApproachState
                          → NeonEdge visual adapter

physical landing
       ↓
Platform.on_ball_landed()
       ↓
landing_occurred
       ↓
LandingFeedbackController
       ↓
LandingEvent
       ↓
future:
 ┌────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┐
 Ball   Particles   Combo    Score   Camera  Audio
```

This is deliberately based around signals because Godot's signals are intended to let objects react to events without hard-wiring them together, which keeps the system flexible as the scene grows. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/getting_started/step_by_step/signals.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### What moved out of `platform.gd`

The important part of the system we just spent all that time tuning is now separated.

`landing_feedback_controller.gd` owns the **decision-making**:

- ballistic landing prediction
- the deterministic horizontal acceleration/deceleration prediction
- target selection
- target hysteresis
- target changes
- retraction coordination
- landing-event emission

`landing_approach_state.gd` owns the **reversible visual timeline**:

- `0 → 20 → 50 → 70 → 80 → 100`
- width-dependent pacing
- edge-dependent pacing
- final catch-up behavior
- target-position smoothing
- retraction
- charge shaping

`platform.gd` is now primarily the platform itself plus a very small **landing-feedback adapter**.

So the NeonEdge path is now:

```text
prediction
   ↓
LandingFeedbackController
   ↓
LandingApproachState
   ↓
platform.set_landing_approach_feedback()
   ↓
NeonEdge shader
```

The shader itself was **not changed**.

That is important: the NeonEdge we know is working remains the same visual implementation. We've simply moved the logic deciding when/how it gets charged out of the platform's main gameplay script.

### The new `LandingEvent`

`scripts/landing/landing_event.gd`

This is the common payload that future systems can consume.

It currently carries things such as:

```text
ball
platform
landing_world_x
landing_ratio
edge_factor
horizontal_velocity
vertical_velocity
approach_progress
platform_type
```

That means the future Perfect/Clutch/combo system won't need to calculate these independently.

For example:

```text
actual landing
      ↓
LandingEvent
      ├── "landing_ratio = 0.51"
      ├── "edge_factor = 0.12"
      ├── "horizontal_velocity = ..."
      └── "approach_progress = ..."
```

Then the quality system can decide:

> GOOD / EPIC / PERFECT / CLUTCH

without knowing anything about how the prediction system works.

### One detail I intentionally handled carefully

`Platform.on_ball_landed()` emits `landing_occurred` **before** completing its local approach state.

That means the `LandingEvent` can capture the actual approach state immediately before physical contact rather than always seeing `1.0`.

Then the platform completes the state and performs the existing landing response.

So we're establishing the exact boundary we talked about:

```text
PREDICTION
    ↓
APPROACH
    ↓
PHYSICAL LANDING
    ↓
LANDING EVENT
    ↓
REACTIONS
```

That's the foundation I wanted.

### What remains untouched

I did **not** modify:

`ball.gd`

`platform_spawner.gd`

the movement physics

the collision behavior

the platform generation logic

the NeonEdge shader

the current prediction math's gameplay meaning

So this is a refactor around the existing system rather than another attempt to "improve" the system itself.

I also didn't add the ball effect, particles, Good/Epic/Perfect, streaks, camera, etc. yet. Those are now **consumers we can add cleanly on top of this foundation** rather than things we have to cram into `platform.gd`.

One limitation: I could verify the resulting repository files and structure through GitHub, but I don't have Godot itself available in this execution environment, so your local Godot run is still the final runtime verification.

I'd now pull **`13dc1af...`** and do one very simple regression test: play exactly the same landing scenarios that made us declare the previous version stable. The key thing we're checking here is **"does the refactor behave identically?"**, not new functionality.

Yes - based on what you described, **the merge was handled correctly**.

The strongest evidence is actually your runtime test:

- Godot opens normally.
- No compile errors.
- The game starts.
- The existing landing behavior feels **exactly the same as before**.
- The new architecture is present.
- Your Git history contains the expected fixes in a sensible order.

So I would consider the restructuring **successfully integrated**, not a corrupted merge.

### About the `.uid` files

Those are normal Godot-generated resource UID files. Godot uses resource UIDs to keep references to resources stable even if files are moved or renamed. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_resourceuid.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So commits like:

> **landing_approach_state.gd.uid creation**

are not suspicious. If Godot generated them as part of recognizing the new scripts, committing them is fine.

---

# The one debugging error

This:

```text
landing_feedback_controller.gd:135
_get_stable_landing_prediction():
The object does not have any 'meta' values with the key
'_towerjump_landing_feedback_target'.
```

is **not a gameplay failure**.

It's actually very easy to explain.

Our controller uses Godot's object metadata as a little piece of temporary memory:

```text
Ball
 └─ metadata:
      _towerjump_landing_feedback_target
```

The controller asks:

> "Hey Ball, do you already have a platform stored as my current landing-feedback target?"

But **on the very first frame**, that metadata hasn't been created yet.

Godot's `get_meta()` produces an error when the requested metadata doesn't exist and no default is supplied. Godot specifically provides `has_meta()` for checking whether a metadata entry exists first. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.5/classes/class_object.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So what's happening is basically:

```text
Game starts
   ↓
LandingFeedbackController starts
   ↓
"What is my current target?"
   ↓
Ball has no target metadata yet
   ↓
Godot prints error
   ↓
Controller continues
   ↓
Finds the first valid platform
   ↓
Everything works
```

That's why **the game behaves correctly despite the debugger message**.

I would still fix it, though. It's a legitimate small bug in the new architecture: we're asking for metadata before establishing a default.

The clean fix is simply to make `_get_stable_landing_prediction()` check `has_meta()` before calling `get_meta()`, or provide a safe default.

**We should fix that before moving on**, because I don't want us accumulating "harmless" debugger errors that later make real problems harder to spot.

---

# Now the important part: what did we actually build?

The easiest way to understand the new structure is:

```text
                         ┌──────────────────────────┐
                         │ LandingFeedbackController│
                         │                          │
                         │ "What platform are we    │
                         │  approaching?"           │
                         └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                      │
                         controls / updates
                                      │
                                      ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────┐
                         │ LandingApproachState     │
                         │                          │
                         │ "How charged should the │
                         │  approach be right now?" │
                         └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                      │
                              visual values
                                      │
                                      ▼
                         ┌──────────────────────────┐
                         │       platform.gd        │
                         │                          │
                         │ "Show that state on this │
                         │  platform."              │
                         └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                NeonEdge
```

Then, **when the physical landing actually happens**:

```text
Ball lands
   ↓
platform.gd detects landing
   ↓
LandingEvent is created
   ↓
LandingFeedbackController broadcasts it
   ↓
EVERYTHING interested can react
   │
   ├── Ball
   ├── NeonEdge
   ├── Landing particles
   ├── Good / Epic / Perfect
   ├── Score
   ├── Streak
   ├── Camera
   ├── Audio
   └── future systems
```

That's the big architectural win.

---

# 1. `platform.gd` - the platform itself

Think of this as:

> **"I am a platform. I know how a platform behaves and how to display myself."**

It still owns things that genuinely belong to a platform:

- platform type
- width / height
- collision
- moving-platform behavior
- breakable behavior
- spring behavior
- spawning/resetting
- platform geometry
- its shaders
- its NeonEdge
- actually receiving the physical landing

But we removed the complicated question:

> "Which platform is the ball probably going to land on?"

That **doesn't belong inside every platform**.

So `platform.gd` no longer needs to individually figure out the player's predicted landing target.

Instead, it has a relatively thin interface such as:

```text
set_landing_approach_feedback(...)
retract_landing_approach_feedback(...)
complete_landing_approach_feedback(...)
reset_landing_feedback_visual()
```

That's basically the platform saying:

> "Okay, LandingFeedbackController. Tell me what visual state you want and I'll display it."

That's much cleaner.

---

# 2. `landing_feedback_controller.gd` - the brain

This is the most important new layer.

Think:

> **"I watch the ball and the platforms and decide which platform is currently relevant."**

It owns the complicated prediction system we already spent a lot of time getting right.

It handles:

- looking at the ball
- looking at available platforms
- predicting where the ball will land
- determining which platform is the best candidate
- switching targets intelligently
- hysteresis / target stability
- calculating time-to-land
- calculating predicted landing position
- calculating edge factor
- telling the current platform how much to charge
- retracting platforms that are no longer the target
- listening for actual landing events

This is where the **existing proven prediction algorithm now lives**.

That's important because we didn't redesign that system.

We essentially moved it out of `platform.gd` and gave it its own home.

---

# 3. `landing_approach_state.gd` - the little state machine

This one is easier to misunderstand.

It is **not the brain**.

It's more like:

> **"Given what the brain tells me, how should the approach charge progress over time?"**

For example:

```text
Controller says:

Platform A
Time until landing = 0.8 sec
Landing position = 73%
Edge factor = 0.2
```

The `LandingApproachState` takes that information and determines:

```text
progress = 0.00
      ↓
    0.18
      ↓
    0.42
      ↓
    0.71
      ↓
    0.94
      ↓
    1.00
```

It also handles the reversible nature of the charge.

So if the ball stops heading toward Platform A:

```text
██████████████████░░
        ↓
██████████░░░░░░░░░░
        ↓
████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░
```

the charge can retract smoothly instead of the platform being permanently "charged."

It also owns the smoothing of the target position.

So:

**Controller = decides what is happening**

**ApproachState = calculates the progression of that happening**

**Platform = visually applies it**

That's a very useful separation.

---

# 4. `landing_event.gd` - the message

This is perhaps the simplest one.

It doesn't really *do* anything.

It's a **package of information**.

When the actual landing happens, we can say:

> "A landing just happened. Here are all the facts about it."

For example:

```text
LandingEvent

ball
platform
landing_world_x
landing_ratio
edge_factor
horizontal_velocity
vertical_velocity
approach_progress
platform_type
```

So later we can have:

```text
LandingEvent
     │
     ├── Score system
     │      → +25
     │
     ├── Quality system
     │      → EPIC
     │
     ├── Particle system
     │      → burst direction
     │
     ├── Ball
     │      → glow
     │
     ├── Camera
     │      → subtle impact
     │
     ├── Streak system
     │      → streak +1
     │
     └── Audio
            → landing sound
```

None of those systems need to start digging around inside `platform.gd` to figure out what happened.

That's **exactly why the event exists**.

---

# And where is NeonEdge now?

This is the nice part:

## The actual NeonEdge visual is still part of the platform.

So we didn't move the shader somewhere weird.

The chain is currently:

```text
LandingFeedbackController
          │
          │ "Platform X should be
          │  72% charged"
          ▼
LandingApproachState
          │
          │ progress = 0.72
          │ target_x = ...
          ▼
platform.gd
          │
          │ set shader uniforms
          ▼
NeonEdge
          │
          ▼
actual glowing platform edge
```

And the shader remains:

```text
platform_edge_feedback.gdshader
```

So **NeonEdge itself is still the visual implementation**.

That's good.

We don't want the controller drawing neon.

The controller shouldn't care whether the platform uses:

- NeonEdge
- particles
- a sprite
- a shader
- animated geometry
- something completely different

Its job is simply to communicate the state.

---

# Where will the future features live?

This is where the new architecture becomes really valuable.

### Ball glow

Eventually something like:

```text
LandingEvent
      ↓
Ball landing feedback
      ↓
ball shader / glow
```

Not stuffed into `platform.gd`.

---

### Landing particles

```text
LandingEvent
      ↓
LandingParticleController
      ↓
6-12 geometric energy fragments
```

And because the event contains horizontal velocity, the particle system can know:

> "The ball was moving right."

and bias the burst accordingly.

---

### Good / Epic / Perfect

Potentially:

```text
LandingEvent
      ↓
LandingQualityEvaluator
      ↓
GOOD / EPIC / PERFECT
```

The evaluator can look at:

- approach progress
- landing ratio
- edge factor
- maybe velocity
- maybe future timing information

And then produce:

```text
LandingQuality.GOOD
LandingQuality.EPIC
LandingQuality.PERFECT
```

That result can then drive several other things.

---

### Score

```text
LandingEvent
     ↓
ScoreSystem
     ↓
+10 / +25 / +50
```

---

### Streak

```text
LandingEvent
     ↓
StreakSystem
     ↓
3 → stronger feedback
5 → stronger
8 → stronger
...
```

---

### Camera

```text
LandingEvent
     ↓
CameraFeedback
     ↓
tiny impact / zoom / movement
```

---

### Audio

Same idea:

```text
LandingEvent
     ↓
LandingAudio
     ↓
sound based on quality
```

---

# So the philosophy is basically this

Before:

```text
platform.gd
 ├── platform gameplay
 ├── platform visuals
 ├── prediction
 ├── targeting
 ├── approach timing
 ├── landing detection
 ├── future effects
 ├── score?
 ├── particles?
 ├── camera?
 └── everything else?
```

That becomes a nightmare.

Now:

```text
platform.gd
 ├── platform gameplay
 ├── platform-specific visuals
 └── landing adapter

landing_feedback_controller.gd
 └── landing prediction / targeting brain

landing_approach_state.gd
 └── approach progression state

landing_event.gd
 └── landing information package

future systems
 ├── ball feedback
 ├── particles
 ├── quality
 ├── score
 ├── streak
 ├── camera
 └── audio
```

**That's the architecture we actually wanted.**

And most importantly: we haven't changed the gameplay behavior you just tested. We've mainly changed **who is responsible for what**.

That means we now have a much safer foundation for adding the "beautiful landing moment" without turning `platform.gd` into a 1,500-line monster.

### One thing I would do next

Before adding *any* new visual feature, I'd make one tiny cleanup commit for that `get_meta()` startup error.

It isn't evidence that the merge is broken; it's simply the controller querying its optional "current target" metadata before that metadata exists. Godot explicitly distinguishes `has_meta()` from `get_meta()`, and `get_meta()` without a default logs an error when the key is absent. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.6/classes/class_object.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

After that, I'd consider the **architecture milestone completely clean** and only then start building the actual landing-event reactions.

---

**Sources:**

- [ResourceUID — Godot Engine (latest) documentation in English](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/classes/class_resourceuid.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)


The platform reaction asks:

That's why I separated them.

Godot's signals are particularly appropriate for this boundary because they allow an event to be emitted once and multiple independent systems to react without directly coupling those systems together. ```

still becomes strongly RIGHT.

```text
RIGHT LEFT RIGHT LEFT
```

doesn't make the predicted landing point teleport back and forth.

Only the visual landing prediction becomes less sensitive to control jitter.

I think this is probably the single cleanest improvement.

This is the second part, and I think it directly solves your:

> "I'm 10–20 px above the platform, wildly steering, and suddenly the system has no idea what to do."

Once we've already committed to a platform and we're close to landing, I don't think we should allow the target identity to fluctuate freely anymore.

```text
normal flight
    ↓
target acquired
    ↓
approach progressing
    ↓
time-to-land < ~450ms
    ↓
┌───────────────────────────┐
│ LANDING COMMITMENT WINDOW │
└───────────────────────────┘
    ↓
small prediction changes
→ IGNORE
```

So if the system is at:

and the player does:

we don't suddenly do:

```text
→ target lost
→ target changed
→ retract
→ new target
→ charge
→ snap
```

Instead:

```text
→ target point moves smoothly
→ charge continues cautiously
→ actual landing resolves it
```

That is **much more like a human interpretation of the player's intent**.

This is important.

We previously learned that overly strong locking can be just as bad.

### Temporary prediction failure

Keep current target briefly.

### Wild steering reversal

Only after the old target has been clearly invalid for a short sustained period:

while still allowing it to move meaningfully when the player's actual trajectory genuinely changes.

**prediction remains based on reality**

Done. I implemented the **small safeguard we agreed on**, while deliberately avoiding the mistakes from the previous over-cautious version.

I added a dedicated layer:

`scripts/landing/landing_prediction_filter.gd`

and integrated it into the existing `LandingFeedbackController`.

Latest commits:

- `dd2577dd1ab20a08d8f12bb2fede7d62c9c91d0f` - adds the visual prediction filter
- `7832828d77b4421ed35e691e2a765bdc9089f381` - integrates the short target-loss grace
- `a9689d534c09d2a1e60b9766739bda4f947be4e7` - fixes the filter type annotation

### What Experiment A does

The existing target-selection logic stays intact.

When the current target briefly becomes invalid because of a few unstable steering frames, we now keep the **last valid target for only 90 ms** instead of immediately abandoning it.

So:

```text
target valid
→ 60%
→ prediction briefly disappears
→ keep target for a few frames
→ prediction returns
→ continue normally
```

rather than:

```text
60%
→ target lost
→ retract
→ reacquire
→ compressed landing
→ snap
```

Crucially, this does **not freeze the charge** and does not create a larger landing zone.

### What Experiment B does

The new `LandingPredictionFilter` only touches the **visual predicted X**.

It does not modify:

- ball physics
- steering
- time-to-land
- platform selection
- approach progress

It takes:

```text
raw predicted X
+
previous filtered X
+
response rate
```

and filters rapid oscillation.

So something like:

```text
55 → 45 → 65 → 40 → 70
```

won't make the visual target jump around at full amplitude.

But a sustained change such as:

```text
RIGHT
RIGHT
RIGHT
RIGHT
RIGHT
```

still moves the target quickly toward the new position.

The filter specifically detects rapid reversals and reduces its **visual response rate**, rather than filtering the player's actual steering input. That is the distinction we learned from the previous failed experiment.

### Most importantly

I did **not** add:

- feedback steering-input smoothing
- uncertainty mode
- "uncertain = stop charging"
- broad reachability envelopes
- a larger global landing margin
- aggressive new target locking
- any changes to `ball.gd`

So the intended philosophy is:

> **Stabilize the interpretation, not the gameplay and not the progression.**

And the current progression system remains the one you already liked.

Yes - I think both issues are real, and I would **not revert the new version**. The important part is that the new filter is directionally helping; we just pushed the stabilization a little too far, and there is also a concrete bug in the new 90 ms grace implementation.

## 1. Rapid `→ ← → ← →` steering: I think we're double-smoothing

Looking at the current code, the visual prediction goes through **two smoothing layers**:

`raw predicted X`
→ `LandingPredictionFilter`
→ `LandingApproachState._set_target_x()`

And both become especially conservative during exactly the situation you're describing.

The new filter can drop from a response of `28` down toward `10`, while the approach state itself can drop from `10` down to `5` near landing.

So during rapid steering we're effectively telling the system:

> "Don't react too much to this movement."

and then immediately:

> "Also, don't react too much to the already-filtered movement."

That explains why the new version feels somewhat better against tabbing, but sometimes develops that **30 → 100 / 0 → 100 feeling** on small platforms. The system isn't necessarily failing to understand the jump; it can simply be **too late visually in accepting the updated target**.

### I would tune, not remove, the filter

I'd move it toward something like:

```gdscript
NORMAL_RESPONSE := 36.0
OSCILLATION_RESPONSE := 18.0
REVERSAL_WINDOW := 0.12
REVERSAL_DECAY := 5.0
REVERSAL_GAIN := 0.35
```

The idea is:

- normal movement becomes noticeably faster
- oscillation is still damped
- reversal memory disappears faster
- each reversal has less influence
- a genuine 300-500 ms directional hold quickly becomes treated as real intent

That last point is important. A player doing:

`→ ← → ← →`

for 50-100 ms each direction should be treated differently from:

`→ → → → →`

for 300-500 ms.

Our current filter recognizes the difference, but it carries the "oscillation penalty" for too long.

### And I'd relax the second smoothing layer too

I'd also change:

```gdscript
APPROACH_TARGET_SMOOTH_RATE := 10.0
APPROACH_TARGET_SMOOTH_RATE_NEAR_LANDING := 5.0
```

to something more like:

```gdscript
APPROACH_TARGET_SMOOTH_RATE := 16.0
APPROACH_TARGET_SMOOTH_RATE_NEAR_LANDING := 9.0
```

So we have **one meaningful stabilizer**, rather than two heavily damped ones fighting each other.

That should preserve the nice "rapid steering doesn't make the indicator twitch everywhere" behavior without making the indicator feel sluggish.

---

# 2. The long reversed-U + edge landing problem has an actual bug

This one is even clearer.

The controller currently intends to do:

> stable target briefly loses precise prediction → hold last valid prediction for 90 ms → don't destroy the sequence.

But the code doesn't actually do that in the situation you're hitting.

Inside `_get_stable_landing_prediction()` we have:

```gdscript
if stable_target != null and stable_target.visible:
    var current_prediction := _get_platform_prediction(
        _ball,
        stable_target
    )

    if not current_prediction.is_empty():
        ...
    
    return best_prediction
```

Then **after that whole branch** comes the 90 ms grace logic.

So when the current target is still known, but `_get_platform_prediction()` temporarily returns `{}` - which is exactly what can happen on those aggressive edge approaches - the function reaches:

```gdscript
return best_prediction
```

**before the grace section is ever reached.**

So the 90 ms safeguard isn't protecting the exact failure case we introduced it for.

That is a genuine implementation mistake, not just tuning.

---

# What I'd do for issue 2

I'd fix that control flow first.

The intended order should be:

### Stable target exists
1. Precise prediction valid → use it normally.
2. Precise prediction temporarily invalid → **use last valid prediction for up to 90 ms.**
3. Only after that grace expires → allow target replacement.

That alone should already eliminate a large portion of those sudden:

**`0 → 100`**

edge landings.

---

## But I think we should add one more small safeguard specifically for the edge case

Because your reversed-U jump is a particularly nasty scenario:

> long arc → approach from above → keep holding a direction → arrive almost exactly at the platform edge.

```text
        ↓

        ↓
```


The important part is that the fallback requires **all of those conditions**.

For example, conceptually:

```text
    YES
Ball descending?
    YES
Target below ball?
    YES

```

```text
                ball
```

Instead of saying:

we say:

> "Prediction invalid, but we're already committed, descending, almost at the platform, and physically near its corridor → don't abandon the visual target now."

Then the actual collision finishes the sequence.

And importantly, physical collision remains the final authority. Godot's `move_and_slide()` detects collisions during the movement step, and the slide-collision data can be inspected afterward, which fits our architecture of letting the actual landing event determine the final `100%`. ↓
```text
ball shoots upward
↓
A is now above the ball
↓
A.y < ball.y
↓
late fallback cannot activate
```

```text
↓

↓
```

```text
A becomes above ball → fallback impossible
↓
B becomes target normally
↓
B starts charging
```

That should preserve the normal straight-up behavior.

That makes the system more conservative **only at the exact point where target switching is least useful anyway**.

I would **revert the current Step 1 experiment**, not try to rescue it.

Your test results are actually useful because they tell us something pretty specific:

### What we've learned

The current Step 1 did **not** solve the fundamental curved-edge problem.

Scenario 3 still produces:

`long curved approach → continuous steering → edge → sometimes little/no charge → 100%`

And scenario 5 became worse.

At the same time, scenarios 1 and 2 are already excellent:

`normal steer → release → land`  
`normal steer → small late correction → land`

So I don't want to touch the mechanism that makes those cases work.

The important distinction is:

> **The problem isn't that the system doesn't lock a platform generally.**

It locks it very well in ordinary approaches.

The problem is specifically:

> **the ballistic prediction becomes wrong/too uncertain during a long sustained curved approach while the player is still holding a direction, especially when the eventual landing is near the edge.**

That's why your observation:

> "when I release above the edge it works better"

is such a strong clue.

When you release, the prediction switches to the **deceleration model**, which gives it a much more stable future X.

When you continue holding:

```text
hold RIGHT
        ↓
ball is still moving
        ↓
prediction assumes future acceleration / current control
        ↓
long curved trajectory
        ↓
prediction can remain outside the platform corridor
        ↓
no confident target
        ↓
too little time
        ↓
100%
```

So I think we've been attacking the wrong layer with some of the safeguards.

---

# What I would do now

## 1. Revert the current Step 1

The late-commitment fallback was a reasonable idea, but your actual test shows it isn't addressing the root problem.

And I especially don't want to keep it because we now know how dangerous generic "keep the target when prediction is invalid" logic can be.

So I'd go back to the **last stable version before Step 1**.

That preserves:

- excellent straight jumps
- excellent normal steering
- good edge behavior when the approach is stable
- the existing prediction filter
- the existing target smoothing
- all the architecture

---

# 2. Then attack the actual problem differently

I think the next experiment should be much more surgical:

## **Separate "platform eligibility" from "exact landing-point accuracy."**

Right now they're still too closely coupled.

We really have two questions:

### Question A

> **Am I actually approaching this platform?**

### Question B

> **Exactly where on this platform will I land?**

For normal jumps, they line up.

For your long curved edge case, they can diverge.

You can have:

```text
"I'm definitely going to land on Platform B"
```

while:

```text
"my predicted exact X is currently noisy / uncertain"
```

And that's precisely the situation where we currently lose the visual charge.

---

# The experiment I'd test next

Once a platform is already a **strong target**, I would allow the platform to remain eligible even when the exact predicted X briefly wanders outside the visual landing corridor.

But I would **not** give it a big reachability envelope.

Instead we'd use a tiny concept:

```text
TARGET IDENTITY
      ↓
"Yes, we're heading toward B."
      ↓
EXACT X PREDICTION
      ↓
can be noisy
      ↓
visual target gets clamped/smoothed
```

So the system becomes:

```text
platform identity = stable
landing X = flexible
```

rather than:

```text
landing X bad
→ platform identity disappears
```

That's the distinction I think we need.

---

# And importantly, the fallback should be based on the current trajectory direction

For your long curved landing:

```text
          ball
           ●
          ↖
        ↖
      ↖
    ↖
  ↖
-------------------- platform
                    ● edge
```

If the ball is:

- descending
- moving toward the platform's horizontal span
- already committed to that platform
- physically within/near the platform corridor

then the exact future X should **not be allowed to cancel the target completely**.

Instead:

> "The exact landing point is uncertain, but the landing target is still clear."

That's much closer to how a human would interpret it.

---

# And this would also solve the weird release difference

With release:

```text
prediction becomes stable
→ normal path
```

With continuous hold:

```text
prediction remains somewhat uncertain
→ target identity stays stable anyway
→ visual X is allowed to settle gradually
```

So the two situations would behave more similarly.

That's exactly what we want.

---

# I would still keep B/C separate

You were right earlier about the double smoothing.

I would **not touch either smoothing layer in the next experiment**.

We already know the current filter gives some benefit and hasn't caused the catastrophic failure that the other safeguard did.

So:

**revert Step 1**

→ **keep the stable filter**

→ **keep current approach state**

→ test only this new distinction between:

**target identity** vs **exact X prediction**

If that works, *then* we can decide whether we even need to tune the filter further.

---

## So my recommendation is very clear

**Revert the current Step 1.**

Don't add more safeguards to it.

Then make the next experiment specifically target this:

> **Once a platform is already strongly identified, temporary uncertainty in the exact landing X should not make the platform cease to be the target.**

That is much narrower than the previous "prediction lost → keep target" idea, and it directly addresses the long curved edge case without touching the excellent behavior of your normal jumps.

Latest commits:

`52afbb252cc4b8e4b564dc11934422a05620ab00` — **Separate landing target identity from exact X prediction**  
`414166806c07a0114cfd338d36a79a1e12f90154` — **Remove redundant landing target X smoothing**

I also re-fetched both files afterward and verified the intended structure is present.

### What changed

**Target identity is now separated from exact landing X.**

When the current target is already established and its exact predicted X briefly becomes invalid, the controller can now keep that platform as the target **only if**:

- it already had meaningful approach progress
- the ball is descending
- the platform is below the ball
- landing is within a limited `0.65s` window
- the ball is physically within or very close to the platform's real landing corridor
- when just outside the physical corridor, the ball must actually be moving back toward the platform

The fallback is only for the **existing target**. It cannot create a new target.

This means:

```text
TARGET B
  ↓
exact X prediction gets noisy
  ↓
"we're still clearly heading toward B"
  ↓
keep B
```

instead of:

```text
exact X prediction noisy
  ↓
B disappears as target
  ↓
sequence dies
  ↓
100% on landing
```

And I deliberately removed the old generic `TARGET_LOSS_GRACE_TIME` logic entirely, because we already learned that a broad "prediction disappeared → hold target" rule can interfere with normal platform handoff.

### No more double X smoothing

You were right about this.

`LandingPredictionFilter` is now the **single smoothing layer** for predicted landing X.

`LandingApproachState` now directly uses the filtered target:

```text
raw prediction
    ↓
LandingPredictionFilter
    ↓
filtered X
    ↓
LandingApproachState
    ↓
direct target X
```

There is no second `lerp()` smoothing layer afterward.

So we now have exactly the separation we wanted:

**Target identity = stable**

**Exact X = responsive but filtered once**

**Visual progress = unaffected**

**Ball physics = untouched**

That is the cleanest version of this experiment we've had so far.

## One concrete issue I spotted while reviewing the physics

There's a potential mismatch between the controller's predicted landing time and the actual collision geometry.

In url`landing_feedback_controller.gd`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/main/scripts/landing/landing_feedback_controller.gd, the prediction calculates vertical time using the platform's **center Y**\. But the ball lands when its bottom reaches the platform's **top edge**\.

With the current values—a ball radius of 30 px and platform height of 20 px—that means the actual collision happens when the ball's center is approximately **40 px above the platform center**\. The controller's predicted landing time can therefore extend beyond the real contact time.

That is a plausible contributor to the charge being behind when the landing occurs. It does not, by itself, explain the rapid-tapping problem, so I don't want to claim we've found the complete solution.

## How we should proceed

Let's keep these as two separate problems\:

- **Long curved approach and edge landing\:** verify that the predicted landing time matches the actual collision surface, so the charge timeline is working toward the right contact moment.
- **Rapid left/right tapping\:** separate the identity of the platform being approached from the exact predicted landing X. The current prediction assumes the present steering input continues until landing, which becomes unreliable when the player keeps reversing direction.

The next experiment should change **only the contact-time calculation**, leaving the restored smoothing and target-selection logic untouched. We can test that independently before changing the rapid-tapping behavior.

And I agree with your broader point: steering freely is fundamental to TowerJump. The feedback system needs to handle that behavior consistently instead of relying on players not discovering its weak spots.

You're right to challenge the proposed contact-time change before we try it. We've already run several experiments, and another plausible-sounding fix isn't enough. We need to identify which part of the system causes each failure and choose a change that actually addresses that mechanism.

## 1\. First, the target-loss grace should go

The restored `a9689...` controller **does contain the 0.09-second target-loss grace behavior**\. It remembers the last valid prediction and temporarily reuses it when the current target's prediction disappears.

Given our previous tests and your explicit decision not to keep that generic grace, we should remove it rather than quietly carrying it forward. It doesn't solve the underlying prediction problem; it only postpones the moment when the system reacts to a missing prediction.

There's an important distinction, though: removing grace should not mean that the system has to forget the target whenever the predicted landing X briefly changes. We still need to solve that problem directly, without retaining a stale prediction simply because it was valid a few frames ago.

## 2\. Would correcting contact time solve the two failures?

**It could help the charge timing, but it cannot by itself solve both failures.** Here's why.

The current controller calculates time to the platform's *center*\:

$$
t_{\text{current}}=
\frac{-v_y+\sqrt{v_y^2+2g\,\Delta y}}{g}
$$

But the ball contacts the platform before its center reaches the platform center. With a 30 px ball radius and a 20 px platform height, the top collision surface is about 40 px above the platform center.

The relevant vertical target for predicting contact is therefore\:

$$
y_{\text{contact}}=
y_{\text{platform}}-\frac{h_{\text{platform}}}{2}-r_{\text{ball}}
$$

That distinction matters because `LandingApproachState` uses `time_to_land` to decide how quickly to charge. If the controller overestimates the remaining time, the charge can progress too slowly and still need to jump to 100% when the actual landing event completes it.

Godot's `CharacterBody2D` detects contact during `move_and_slide()`, and your actual bounce is triggered by that collision; the visible 8 px NeonEdge doesn't change the collision shape. citeturn377290search1turn377290search3

So your slow-motion inspection is relevant: it supports that the actual collision looks correct. The potential mismatch is in the controller's *prediction*, not necessarily the collision itself.

But this is only a timing issue. It doesn't explain why rapid direction reversals sometimes cause the controller to select no platform at all.

## 3\. The rapid-tapping failure has a more direct explanation in the code

After checking the current controller and both helper scripts, I think we should focus on one specific interaction.

The current system does three things in this order\:

1. **Predicts the platform.** `_get_platform_prediction()` estimates where the ball will be when it reaches the platform.
2. **Rejects the candidate if the predicted X is outside the landing corridor.** The permitted range is the platform's half-width plus the ball radius.
3. **Smooths the X position for the visuals.** `LandingPredictionFilter` only runs after a valid platform prediction has been selected.

That order matters.

The horizontal prediction assumes the ball continues following its *current* steering direction for the entire remaining time to landing. That's a reasonable approximation for a sustained hold, but not necessarily for repeated left-right taps.

Imagine this sequence\:

**The player reverses direction**

The projected landing point jumps because the controller assumes the latest direction will continue until landing.

---

**The prediction leaves the corridor**

`_get_platform_prediction()` returns an empty dictionary. The visual filter never gets a chance to smooth that rejected prediction.

---

**The target disappears**

The controller can clear the selected target, causing the approach charge to retract. If the platform is selected again later, the charge resumes from a lower value.

---

**Physical landing completes the animation**

The actual landing event forces progress to 100%, making the interruption visible as a snap.

This explains why changing the smoothing constants alone hasn't fixed the underlying issue. **The system can lose the platform before the smoothing layer is even involved.**

## 4\. So how much would correcting contact time help?

It has a more meaningful effect than simply making the charge animation finish sooner.

The current estimate targets the platform center, but the actual landing occurs at the collision surface. Using the actual contact height would shorten the estimated remaining time. That would affect two things simultaneously\:

- **Charge timing\:** the controller would know that contact is closer and could increase charge at the appropriate rate.
- **Horizontal prediction\:** the controller would project the ball's motion over a shorter interval. That matters because the current input direction is assumed to persist for that entire interval.

For a long curved approach ending near an edge, the shorter and more accurate projection could stop the controller from predicting a landing point beyond the valid corridor even though the ball will actually touch the edge.

For rapid tapping, it could also reduce the size of the jumps in predicted X. But it cannot remove the underlying assumption that the *latest* direction will persist until contact. If the direction changes repeatedly, that prediction can still jump in and out of the corridor.

So my conclusion is\:

| Test case | What contact-time correction could do |
|--------|--------|
| Long curved approach → edge landing | Directly addresses the incorrect prediction horizon, so it could fix or substantially improve this case. |
| Small/normal platform → rapid tapping | Could reduce the instability, but it is not enough to guarantee stable target selection. |

I would not claim that this one change fixes both cases before you test it.

## 5\. The next experiments should be isolated

The generic grace has now been removed in a new commit\:

url**Remove generic landing target-loss grace — `6be4145`**https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/commit/6be414506742ebc2c0bb041af20be9649bc6bb01

**Please pull once more in GitHub Desktop** before testing, because that commit was made after your previous pull. I haven't run the project in Godot, so this change still needs runtime verification.

After that, I recommend proceeding in this order.

**Experiment A — Correct the contact-time calculation only.** Use the top collision surface and ball radius to determine the predicted contact time. Use that same time for both charge timing and horizontal projection. Leave the target filter, smoothing, target selection, and progress behavior otherwise untouched. Test both of your problem cases, plus the two normal landing scenarios that already work.

**Experiment B — Address unstable target identity if tapping still causes it.** The controller must stop treating one exact projected X as the sole condition for whether a platform is a valid target. But we also must not return to the broad reachability envelope that activated unrelated platforms during otherwise ordinary jumps.

The next design needs to distinguish the identity of a plausible landing platform from the exact X position used to animate its charge. It should use current physics and ongoing steering evidence to decide whether the platform remains a plausible target, while the visual X can respond continuously to changing direction. That should be a live assessment, not a generic grace timer or an indefinitely reused old prediction.

I would investigate that as a separate change, not combine it with Experiment A.

This gives us a way to reason about the outcome: if contact-time correction improves the edge case but tapping still causes target loss, we'll have isolated the remaining problem to the prediction/selection logic rather than continuing to tweak charge timing blindly.

## My recommendation: a narrow, current-target-only Experiment B

I would **not** make the prediction corridor wider for every platform. That risks bringing back the earlier behavior where unrelated platforms start charging during ordinary jumps.

Instead, the experiment should distinguish two decisions\:

- **Which platform are we approaching?** This is about the identity of the target.
- **Where should the charge converge on that platform?** This is about the predicted landing position.

Right now, these decisions are too tightly coupled: if the point prediction falls outside the corridor, `_get_platform_prediction()` returns `{}`, and the controller can lose the target completely.

### The proposed behavior

(Keep unchanged)

**Target acquisition**

A new platform must still pass the current strict prediction test before it can become the target. No global expansion of the prediction corridor.

---

(Experiment B)

**Preserve the current target when appropriate**

If the existing target's exact projected landing X temporarily fails, calculate whether that same platform remains physically reachable before contact. Recalculate this every physics frame rather than reusing an old prediction.

---

(Experiment B)

**Keep the visual sequence coherent**

If the current target remains plausible, don't retract its charge solely because the point estimate briefly crossed outside the corridor. Use a bounded visual estimate for the landing point, while leaving the charge progression and smoothing rules unchanged.

---

(Safety condition)

**Still allow genuine target changes**

If the existing platform is no longer physically plausible, or another platform becomes clearly preferable under the existing selection rules, the controller can release or switch the target. The mechanism must not lock onto a platform indefinitely.

The critical distinction is that **reachability would preserve an already selected target; it would not allow every nearby platform to start charging**\.

This is also different from the generic 0.09-second grace behavior we removed. It doesn't simply freeze a stale prediction for a fixed duration. And I would not reapply the previous committed-target fallback verbatim: that version was limited to late descent and a very narrow position range, so it could fail before the ball reached that final window.

## Why this is worth testing now

Your results suggest that Experiment A corrected an important part of the timing model: the charge has much less snapping during rapid tapping, while normal jumps remain stable. Godot's `CharacterBody2D` still handles the physical collision during movement, separately from our controller's estimate of when that collision will happen. citeturn895914search1

Experiment B would address the remaining problem at a different layer: **temporary loss of target identity when the current point estimate becomes unreliable**\.

I’ve created a separate branch, url`experiment-b-target-identity`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/tree/experiment-b-target-identity, starting from the corrected contact-time baseline. **`main` remains untouched by Experiment B**, and the branch is ready for the isolated implementation. We should leave the current clean baseline alone until the branch passes your four tests.

One detail I'd preserve during implementation: the reachability test should use the ball's current horizontal velocity, its acceleration and speed limits, the corrected time to contact, and the platform's actual contact corridor. It should not assume the latest left/right input is guaranteed to continue until landing—that is precisely the assumption that becomes unreliable during rapid tapping.

**That's the next experiment I'd run.** It directly targets the remaining failure mechanism without changing the charge timing, removing the current smoothing, or widening the rules for initially selecting platforms.

**Yes, I think this is fixable without spending hours rebuilding the landing system.** The important part is that we should not try to force the existing animation to behave identically at every pace. We should make it respond intelligently to how much time remains before contact.

I inspected the current implementation on your `experiment-b-target-identity` branch, and I think we have a specific reason to investigate before considering a larger redesign.

## 1\. Why fast approaches expose the weakness

Your system already tries to accelerate its charge when landing approaches. The problem is that several parts of the progression algorithm limit how quickly it can respond.

In url`landing_approach_state.gd`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/experiment-b-target-identity/scripts/landing/landing_approach_state.gd, the current behavior is roughly\:

- Preferred charge duration is **0.9–1.35 seconds**, depending on platform width, with an additional allowance for edge approaches.
- The desired charging rate is calculated from the remaining progress and predicted landing time.
- However, the rate is capped at **2.25 times the preferred rate**\.
- The charging rate itself also changes gradually, rather than immediately reaching the required rate.
- Actual physical contact sets the progress to 100%, regardless of how much charging was completed beforehand.

The last behavior is intentional: physical contact must always win. But combined with the rate limits, it explains how the visual charge can remain low until impact and then jump straight to 100%. The url`landing_feedback_controller.gd`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/experiment-b-target-identity/scripts/landing/landing_feedback_controller.gd already handles target prediction and selection separately, so we don't need to reopen that entire system to investigate this.

## 2\. The solution I would test first

I would introduce **deadline-aware charging**\: the animation keeps its current preferred tempo when there is enough time, but it is allowed to accelerate more aggressively when contact is approaching quickly.

**Normal approach — plenty of time**

Keep the current charging behavior, preserving the result you have already tested and approved.

---

**Fast approach — little time remaining**

Let the desired rate exceed the normal catch-up cap when necessary, make the rate adjustment respond faster, and reduce the fixed time buffer that otherwise leaves too much progress unfinished at contact.

---

**At actual contact**

Keep the existing authoritative completion and white confirmation flash. The experiment changes the approach animation, not the physical landing or bounce.

I would implement these adjustments together as **one narrowly scoped experiment in `LandingApproachState`**, because they address the same underlying issue: the progression controller cannot build charge quickly enough to meet its deadline.

I would not add another grace timer, preserve stale predictions, change platform selection, or introduce another smoothing layer. Those are separate mechanisms, and we have no reason yet to reopen them.

## 3\. Is a 100–200 ms approach window enough?

There is one limitation worth distinguishing from a code defect.

A 100 ms window is only about six frames at 60 FPS. We can accelerate the charge so that it makes meaningful visible progress during that time, but we cannot show the same leisurely, detailed animation that we show over a full second. The fast version must be a **compressed version of the same visual sequence**, not an attempt to fit a one-second animation into 100 ms without changing its character.

The practical goal is to have the bilateral charge visibly advance toward completion before contact, leaving only a small final completion step for the flash. We should not demand a mathematically perfect 100% charge on every frame if doing so makes the effect erratic when the landing prediction changes.

## 4\. How to test this without another long debugging cycle

I'd create one new experiment branch from the currently tested baseline and change only the progression timing.

Then run four focused tests\:

| Test | What we need to confirm |
|--------|--------|
| Normal, widely spaced platforms | The approved charging tempo remains unchanged. |
| Dense platforms, roughly 200 ms of feedback lead time | The charge visibly advances instead of barely moving before contact. |
| Very short lead time, around 100 ms | The charge is substantially advanced at contact, without an obvious 0–100 snap. |
| Rapid steering changes during a fast approach | The charge remains visually stable while the target position adjusts. |

We should also verify that the white confirmation flash still reads clearly and that the charge does not finish prematurely when the predicted landing time changes.

**My recommendation is to try this one experiment before considering a redesign.** The current code already calculates how much progress is needed before landing; the most promising next step is to let that calculation control the charging rate more effectively when time is short. That gives us a concrete hypothesis to test, without disturbing the target-selection work that just became stable.

And we should keep the currently approved baseline untouched until the experiment passes those tests.
