**I agree with your conclusion: I would keep this as an intentional gameplay exception and leave `main` unchanged.** Your explanation identifies a real limitation of the visual timing system, although I'd adjust one detail about why it happens.

## 1\. What's actually happening?

Your sequence is essentially\:

**Jump toward the next platform**

The ball is travelling upward at high speed.

**The edge landing becomes imminent**

The system has very little time to display the approach and charging sequence.

**Contact and bounce happen almost immediately**

The landing event completes the charge, potentially jumping directly to 100%.

The important distinction is that **the platform isn't necessarily failing to detect the ball**\.

Our current controller predicts the landing before contact and drives the approach animation using that prediction. However, if the target only becomes the active approach target shortly before contact, the visual system cannot manufacture extra time that the trajectory doesn't provide.

The implementation also explicitly completes the approach on landing. That sets its progress to `1.0`, which explains the instant snap when the animation hasn't had enough time to finish naturally. See url`landing_feedback_controller.gd`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/main/scripts/landing/landing_feedback_controller.gd and url`landing_approach_state.gd`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/main/scripts/landing/landing_approach_state.gd\.

Godot's physics processing normally runs at a fixed 60 ticks per second, independently of rendering, so extremely short contact windows can leave very few opportunities to advance and display the sequence. citeturn411838search0

## 2\. Could we improve it further?

**Technically, yes. But I don't think we should pursue that right now.**

We could try to start the charge earlier by broadening when an edge landing becomes an eligible target, or by committing to a predicted target sooner. But our existing code already accounts for the ball's radius, allows edge landings, and has a reachability fallback for a target that's already being animated.

Making that prediction more aggressive introduces a different set of problems: the wrong platform might start charging, a target might remain selected when the player can no longer land on it, or charge effects might appear too early. We'd be adding complexity to solve a case where the player has almost no time to see the animation anyway.

We could also invent a special post-contact visual effect, but that would be a new design choice rather than fixing a collision-detection problem.

## 3\. Why I'd keep the snap

Your normal beginning section and the dense-platform stress test are actually demonstrating two different things\:

- **Dense, fast-paced jumps\:** The deadline-aware charging changes make the sequence more consistent across consecutive short approaches. Those changes are already merged into `main`\.
- **Near-zero-window edge chains\:** The ball lands at the edge and immediately rebounds toward another edge. There may simply be insufficient time for the complete charge sequence to be visible.

In the second case, the instant charge can function as a natural visual accent to the unusually fast chain of jumps. It doesn't necessarily need to be eliminated just because it's an exception to the normal animation.

There is one qualification: the current code completes the charge on every landing, rather than explicitly checking that a landing is an ultra-fast edge chain. So we should accept the snap **for the rare cases you've identified**, not declare every instant snap desirable. If we start seeing it on ordinary landings, that would warrant another investigation.

### My decision for the current prototype

Keep the three merged improvements in `main`\. Accept the rare, nearly instantaneous edge-to-edge charge as part of the gameplay rhythm, and don't add another prediction system or special-case mechanism just to eliminate it.

That gives us a stable baseline, preserves the improvements we've already verified, and avoids spending more time on a visual sequence that the player barely has time to perceive in these exceptional landings.

**Yes, Godot can generate those changes again. You didn't miss a one-time migration.** But there's an important distinction: simply opening the project doesn't guarantee that every scene will be rewritten. The changes can reappear as Godot registers resource UIDs and saves the affected scenes or resources.

Here's what that means for TowerJump.

- **UIDs added\:** These give Godot stable resource identifiers, helping references survive file renames or moves. Godot can generate resource UIDs automatically. citeturn163587search6turn163587search1
- **Default values removed\:** This is normal serialization. Godot's scene format omits properties that equal their defaults, and explicitly written defaults are discarded when the scene is saved. citeturn434610search0

I also checked the current url`main` version of `scenes/main.tscn`https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/blob/main/scenes/main.tscn\. It already contains UIDs for many resource references, but a few references still use file paths without UIDs. So a similar editor-generated diff may appear again when those resources are saved.

### What I'd do now

1. Update your local project from `main`\.
2. Open it with the Godot 4.7 version you're using and let the initial scan finish.
3. If Godot marks files as modified, inspect the diff before deciding whether to commit it.

If the changes are limited to generated UID metadata and removal of explicit default values, they're generally normal editor serialization changes—not a replay of our two landing-charge commits. I'd keep those changes separate in their own cleanup commit rather than mix them with gameplay changes. And don't commit the `.godot/` cache.

**Bottom line\:** You haven't lost the merged landing-charge improvements. The serialization changes can be regenerated, and there's no need to recreate or re-merge either of those commits.

I think this is exactly the kind of milestone I'd do next, **before adding the ball's own anticipation and landing feedback system**\.

We've just finished a fairly intricate gameplay-adjacent visual system. Ambient particles give us a chance to improve the game's atmosphere with much less complexity, and the effect will be present during practically every jump rather than only at particular events.

I'd approach this as a small, isolated visual experiment called **Ambient Life v1 — Floating Motes**\.

## The concept

Imagine the current TowerJump scene, but instead of the background feeling completely static, there are tiny particles suspended in the atmosphere. As the ball climbs, you pass through this field of particles.

They drift gently, vary slightly in size and brightness, and occasionally catch the light. Nothing flies directly at the player, and there are no complicated animated objects. The environment simply feels less empty.

The intended feeling is **quiet movement and depth, not a shower of glowing effects**\.

## 1\. How I'd implement it

**One ambient particle emitter**

Use a single `GPUParticles2D` node with a `ParticleProcessMaterial`\. Godot already provides the emission, movement, lifetime and appearance controls we need, without requiring separate game objects or a custom particle simulation. citeturn156475search0turn156475search4

---

**Particles that float, not rush**

Give them slow, slightly varied sideways drift and almost no intrinsic vertical movement. With particles living in world space while the camera follows the ball upwards, the environment naturally scrolls past them. Godot's `local_coords` setting supports this world-space behaviour. citeturn156475search0

---

**Atmosphere behind the gameplay**

Draw them above the background but behind the platforms and ball. They won't collide with anything, change jump behaviour, affect targeting or interact with the charge sequence.

## 2\. My starting settings

These would be initial tuning values, not final requirements.

| Property | Starting point |
|--------|--------|
| Active particle count | About 25–35 |
| Lifetime | 7–12 seconds |
| Visual size | Roughly 1–3 screen pixels |
| Movement | Slow drift with random variation |
| Appearance | Soft dots with varied opacity |
| Color | Muted cyan-blue, with a little cool white |
| Glow | Very subtle; most particles should not look luminous |
| Collision and trails | None |

We can reuse the existing soft-particle texture if it looks appropriate at this scale. Otherwise, a simple soft dot is enough; **there's no need to start another asset-production pipeline**\.

I'd also keep the field relatively sparse. The ball, platform silhouettes and neon landing feedback must remain the stars of the scene. Particles should never be mistaken for coins, platform edges or gameplay indicators.

## 3\. Why this is a good next milestone

The important part is that the first version needs to answer just one question\:

**Does a subtle, moving atmosphere make TowerJump feel more alive without making the gameplay harder to read?**

We don't need different particle types, biomes, environmental interactions or theme-specific effects yet. One emitter can establish whether the idea works before we invest further.

I'd evaluate it in three situations: while the camera is stationary, during a normal ascent, and during a rapid sequence of jumps. That should tell us whether the particles feel naturally suspended in the world, whether the upward camera movement creates the intended sense of travel, and whether anything becomes distracting during intense gameplay.

If the effect works, we can preserve it as a reusable atmospheric layer and make the particle tint configurable for future themes. If it doesn't, we can adjust or remove it without touching the gameplay systems.

## 4\. What I'd deliberately leave for later

I would not combine this with the ball's own visual anticipation system, platform reactions, particle bursts on landings, camera effects or environmental hazards. Those all introduce separate design decisions.

The next milestone should be just **ambient atmosphere**\: one emitter, one material, a restrained appearance, and no gameplay logic changes.

My recommendation is to prototype this on a separate branch from the current `main`, compare it directly against the existing scene, and keep it only if the difference is noticeable in a positive way. That gives us a fresh visual improvement without putting the stable landing-feedback work at risk.

The fact that the motes already make the game feel more alive is a good sign for this direction. We can build atmosphere gradually without adding new gameplay mechanics or making the scene visually busy.

I’ve made a new experiment on the existing **`experiment-ambient-floating-motes` branch**\. `main` is untouched, and I changed only `scenes/main.tscn`\.

## 1\. What I changed

**More noticeable size variation**

The original size range was `0.24-0.45`\. I widened it to `0.18-0.62`, so some motes should look like tiny distant specks while others have a more noticeable soft halo. In Godot, these values define the initial scale range applied to each particle. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/classes/class_particleprocessmaterial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Occasional brighter motes**

I added a separate layer containing just **8 highlight motes**\. They use a brighter cyan-blue tint and a stronger opacity ramp, so they should stand out from the ordinary motes without making every particle bright.

**More activity in the upper half**

The highlight layer spawns mostly in the upper half of the screen. That gives the space above the ball more visual activity while leaving the original motes distributed across the broader area.

The new commit is url**Add size variation and upper-atmosphere mote highlights**https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/commit/2c6ca6b11bfe09ebe4c9ec74ade4702db82752a8\.

Fetch and pull the latest changes on `experiment-ambient-floating-motes` before testing. I’ve verified the updated scene text on GitHub, but haven’t run the project through Godot’s renderer here, so the in-game appearance still needs your test.

## 2\. What does Preprocess: 8s mean?

`Preprocess` tells Godot to simulate the particle system as though it had already been running for that amount of time before showing its initial state. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_gpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Your emitter has both\:

- **Lifetime\:** 8 seconds
- **Preprocess\:** 8 seconds

Because those values match, the particle system can begin with an already-populated distribution of motes. Without preprocessing, the scene would start nearly empty and gradually fill as particles are emitted.

**Why can a high value be expensive?**

At the default particle processing rate of 30 simulation steps per second, 8 seconds corresponds to roughly **240 simulation steps** before the initial state is ready. Godot warns that high preprocessing values can cause expensive startup work, particularly for systems with many particles. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_gpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For the current setup, 8 seconds is not automatically a problem. The original layer has 60 particles, and the new highlight layer has only 8. That is a relatively small particle count. The main thing to watch for is a noticeable pause when the game or scene starts, particularly on a lower-powered phone.

I would **keep 8 seconds for now** because you already like the result and a full distribution is desirable immediately. If we later observe startup stutter on a target phone, we can test reducing it to 3-4 seconds.

It does **not** mean the particles move eight seconds faster, and it does not increase their lifetime beyond the configured eight seconds.

## 3\. What does Visibility Rect cover?

Your current values are\:

```text
x: -520
y: -900
width: 1040
height: 1800
```

The rectangle is centered around the particle node’s origin. Because `AmbientMotes` is a child of `GameCamera` at its default position, that origin is the centre of the camera view.

### Viewport dimensions compared with Visibility Rect

| **Area** | **Horizontal** | **Vertical** |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Viewport | 720 px | 1280 px |
| Visibility Rect | 1040 px | 1800 px |
| Extra space on each side | 160 px | 260 px |

So the viewport covers $x=-360$ to $+360$ and $y=-640$ to $+640$, relative to its centre. The visibility rectangle extends farther in each direction.

**Its job is to control particle visibility/culling-not where particles spawn.** Godot uses this rectangle to decide what region must be visible for the particle system to remain active. The extra space helps avoid particles abruptly appearing or disappearing near the screen edge. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_gpuparticles2d.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

## 4\. What does Emission Box Extents mean?

Your original process material has\:

```text
Emission Box Extents:
x: 440
y: 760
z: 1
```

These are **half-sizes**, not the full dimensions. Godot applies each extent in both positive and negative directions from the box’s centre. ([Godot Engine documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/classes/class_particleprocessmaterial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That gives you\:

| Axis | Spawn range | Full dimension |
|--------|--------|--------|
| X | -440 to +440 | 880 px |
| Y | -760 to +760 | 1520 px |
| Z | -1 to +1 | 2 units |

The Z extent has practically no visual significance for this 2D mote effect.

The spawn box is therefore slightly bigger than your `720 × 1280` viewport: it extends about **80 pixels beyond each side and 120 pixels beyond the top and bottom**\.

Here is the key distinction\:

- **Emission Box Extents\:** where new particles are born.
- **Visibility Rect\:** the region Godot uses to decide whether the particle system should remain active.

The visibility rect is larger because particles may move beyond their initial spawn positions.

For the new highlights, I used extents of `Vector3(440, 380, 1)` and an emission offset of `Vector3(0, -340, 0)`\. That places their spawn box around 340 pixels above the emitter’s centre. Its vertical range is approximately **-720 to +40**, so it covers the upper part of the screen with a small margin beyond the top.

## 5\. Why did the original motes look more concentrated near the bottom?

The visibility rect itself does not direct motes toward the bottom. The original spawn area was already roughly centred on the camera, and the particles use a broad direction spread.

With just 60 softly rendered particles distributed over a box larger than the viewport, you can get visible gaps or random clusters. Their low movement speeds also mean they don't travel very far during their lifetimes.

The separate upper highlight layer is a targeted way to increase activity at the top instead of increasing the density everywhere-which could make the whole scene feel cluttered.

## 6\. Other ideas for improving the atmosphere

I’d explore these one at a time, keeping the current restrained look\:

1. **Subtle hue variation\:** let a small number of motes lean slightly toward icy blue or near-white while keeping cyan as the dominant palette.
2. **Near and far layers\:** larger, slightly more visible motes could drift at one speed, while much smaller and fainter motes move at a different speed. That can imply depth without adding detailed background art.
3. **Extremely subtle twinkle\:** a few motes could gently brighten and fade over their lifetime, instead of blinking abruptly.
4. **Very faint atmospheric haze\:** only later, if the scene still feels too empty. It should remain subtle enough that the ball, platforms and landing feedback remain the focus.

For the next test, I’d focus on just the **size differences, brighter highlights and upper-screen distribution**\. If those feel natural in motion, we can decide whether the extra depth layer or twinkle would add anything further.

---

**Sources:**

- [ParticleProcessMaterial — Godot Engine (4.7) documentation in English](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/4.7/classes/class_particleprocessmaterial.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This is the reference for the particles. The tiny squares and diamond-like fragments feel intentional and belong to the motion effect, rather than looking like generic dust. I'd borrow that shape language but give the main trail more volume and softer edges.

**5 — Comet-like motion**

This is the strongest reference for the trail's silhouette. It looks like energy flowing behind a moving character instead of a sealed ribbon attached to it. The curved, separated tails make the movement feel more dynamic and give us room for geometric fragments.

## 2\. The direction I'd prototype

## The ball: a luminous energy core

Reference: concept 2, with concept 4's color character

image_group{"query":["premium stylized 2D glowing electric blue sphere smooth thick luminous rim subtle inner reflection dark navy background","vivid purple violet luminous orb with bright cyan white central energy core smooth circular rim dark background game character"],"aspect_ratio":"4:5","layout":"carousel"}

The ball should remain clearly 2D—not a realistic 3D planet, but not a flat disc either.

I'd give it a more saturated blue-violet inner core, a smooth and slightly thicker rim, a subtle inner reflection and a brighter central light source. A stronger halo would make it feel energetic without relying on extreme bloom.

---

## The trail: a flowing comet

Reference: concept 5's silhouette, with concept 2's light layering

image_group{"query":["smooth curved cyan comet trail bright narrow inner beam broad translucent outer glow split tapered tails dark navy background","stylized electric blue energy ribbon trailing a glowing orb with two thin separated flowing tails elegant 2D game effect"],"aspect_ratio":"5:4","layout":"carousel"}

This is the biggest change I'd make. Instead of one closed, tapered ribbon with a bright outline, the trail would have three visual layers\:

- **Outer halo\:** broad, soft and translucent, with smooth edges.
- **Inner energy stream\:** narrower, brighter and more saturated.
- **Trailing wisps\:** two or three separated, tapering ribbons that follow slightly different curves.

They should all feel like parts of the same energy flow, but the outer edges shouldn't form one rigid, enclosed tube. The wisps and slight asymmetry would make changes in ball direction feel more alive.

---

## The particles: geometric energy fragments

Reference: concept 3

image_group{"query":["minimal glowing cyan diamond and square energy fragments trailing from a luminous orb on dark navy background","small luminous cyan square particles and angular shards floating in a curved comet trail minimalist game visual effects"],"aspect_ratio":"5:4","layout":"carousel"}

I'd replace most of the generic glowing dots around the trail with small squares, diamonds and a few narrow shards.

Their size, rotation and opacity should vary. The brighter fragments would cluster near the ball and the beginning of the trail, while smaller, fainter fragments disperse farther behind it. The ambient motes should remain a separate system of soft, slow dust-like particles.

## 3\. Should purple become the standard design?

I think it's worth testing purple as a candidate for the default ball and trail palette. The violet concept has a distinctive, rich glow, and it would contrast against the cyan platform energy.

I'd test two versions of the *same shape and animation*\:

image_group{"query":["premium electric cyan blue glowing energy orb with curved comet tail and angular geometric fragments dark navy background"],"aspect_ratio":"3:4","layout":"carousel","num_per_query":1}

**Variant A — Electric blue**

A saturated blue core, cyan-white highlights and a blue-cyan trail. Familiar to the current world, but with greater depth and stronger definition.

image_group{"query":["premium violet purple glowing energy orb with curved purple comet tail cyan white highlights and geometric glowing shards dark navy background"],"aspect_ratio":"3:4","layout":"carousel","num_per_query":1}

**Variant B — Violet**

A violet core and purple trail, with restrained icy-blue or white highlights to connect it visually to the cyan environment.

The long-term design should separate the ball's geometry and animation from its palette, so alternative skins can change the colors without requiring a new trail system. Godot can render trails through `GPUParticles2D`'s trail features, but we'd need to inspect your existing implementation before deciding whether to build on that or generate a custom curved trail. citeturn942415search0

## 4\. How I'd approach the implementation

I wouldn't attempt all of these changes at once. The next milestone should be **Ball Visual Prototype v1**, on a separate branch\:

1. Improve the ball's core, rim and glow while retaining its current position, radius, collision and gameplay physics.
2. Redesign the trail as a smooth, layered comet with separated wisps.
3. Replace the trail's generic dots with a controlled mix of geometric fragments.
4. Compare the blue and violet palettes using the same design, then tune the winning direction before connecting it to the ball's future anticipation and landing-confirmation system.

The key is to improve the character's visual identity *before* adding more feedback effects to it. Otherwise, we'd be building new effects around an appearance we're already dissatisfied with.

**My preferred design direction is concept 2's luminous core + concept 5's flowing comet trail + concept 3's geometric fragments, with concept 4's violet palette tested as a serious candidate.** That combination gives us something more dynamic and distinctive without turning the ball into an overly detailed 3D object or the trail into a chaotic particle explosion.

## Ball Comet Visuals — Polish Pass

Branch: `experiment-ball-comet-visuals`

(Committed)

[Open experiment in GitHub](https://github.com/Kryodo/TowerJump/tree/experiment-ball-comet-visuals)

---

What's improved

**Orb integration**

Filled the darker transition around the inner aura so it blends into the outer rim, reduced the rim thickness slightly, and adjusted the electric-blue rim to integrate better with the ball and trail colors.

**Tapered comet trail**

The trail now begins with a narrow connection under the ball, flares into its main energy stream, then tapers away toward the end. The outer aura follows the same profile.

**More visible wisps and continuous motion**

Both wisps have greater independent curvature and separation. I've also added a subtle animated lateral drift to the trail geometry, helping it retain some life around the jump apex when the ball's movement slows down.

**More intentional geometric particles**

The diamond, square and shard emitters now use a separate neutral particle material so the selected palette can tint each shape distinctly. Their counts, sizes, rotation and movement have been adjusted to make the fragments more noticeable.

### What remains unchanged

The changes are confined to these four visual files\:

- `scenes/ball.gdshader`
- `scenes/ball.tscn`
- `scenes/ball_trail_energy.gdshader`
- `scripts/ball_trail.gd`

The ball's movement, gravity, collision radius, bounce behaviour and gameplay logic are untouched. The ambient-mote atmosphere remains included in the branch's `main` baseline.

### How to test it

1. Open GitHub Desktop and click **Fetch origin**\.
2. Switch to `experiment-ball-comet-visuals` and pull the latest changes.
3. Run the game in Godot and inspect the orb's connection to the trail, especially during diagonal movement, rapid steering and the jump apex.
4. In the `TrailVisual` node's Inspector, compare **Electric Blue** and **Rich Violet** under *Visual Palette*\. The latest scene currently selects violet; switch to blue to compare both with the same geometry.
